Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 56, verses 10–11:

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the categories of the children of Adam, the fortunate and the wretched, He divided the fortunate into two groups:

the foremost (al-sabiqun) and the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin). So He said: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾

Scholars differed in explaining this phrase, giving three opinions. The first is that it is a case of verbal emphasis (al-tawkid al-lafzi), and the predicate is His saying: ﴿Those are the ones brought near﴾.

The second is that "the foremost" in the first instance is the subject (mubtada'), and the second is its predicate, in the manner of your saying: "Zayd, Zayd," meaning: Zayd, the one you have heard of, is Zayd, as the poet said:

And as another said:

"I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry is my poetry, when people are people and time is time."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: This is the view of Sibawayh.

The third is that the first is other than the second, and the meaning is: the foremost in this world to the good deeds are the foremost on the Day of Resurrection to the Gardens, and the foremost to faith are the foremost to the Paradises. This is the most apparent view, and Allah knows best.

If it is said: What do you say about the hadith narrated by Imam Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, which he authenticated, from the hadith of Buraydah ibn al-Husayb, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rose in the morning, called Bilal and said:

"O Bilal, by what did you precede me into Paradise? I have never entered Paradise except that I heard your footsteps before me. I entered last night and heard your footsteps before me, and I came upon a lofty, elevated palace of gold. I said: To whom does this palace belong? They said: To an Arab man. I said: I am an Arab. To whom does this palace belong? They said: To a man of Quraysh. I said: I am a Qurashi. To whom does this palace belong? They said: To a man of the Ummah of Muhammad. I said: I am Muhammad. To whom does this palace belong? They said: To 'Umar ibn al-Khattab."

Bilal said: O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I never gave the adhan except that I prayed two rak'ahs afterward, and whenever I was afflicted with a minor impurity I performed wudu' at that time, and I considered that Allah had made two rak'ahs incumbent upon me. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "By these."

It is said: We receive it with acceptance and affirmation, and it does not indicate that anyone precedes the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) into Paradise.

As for Bilal's going before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) into Paradise, it is because Bilal was calling to Allah first through the adhan, so his adhan went before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and thus his entering before him was like that of a chamberlain and a servant.

It has also been narrated in a hadith that "the Prophet (ﷺ) will be raised on the Day of Resurrection with Bilal before him, calling the adhan."

So his going before him is an honor for His Messenger and a display of his nobility and virtue, not a precedence by Bilal. Rather, this precedence is of the same kind as his precedence in performing wudu' and entering the mosque and the like. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 56, verses 18–19:

Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi said: Abdullah ibn Salih narrated to us from Mu'awiyah ibn Salih, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas, regarding the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And a cup from a flowing spring﴾.

He said: "The wine, in which there is no ghawl (harm or intoxicating bane), and it does not cause headache."

And regarding the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Nor will they be intoxicated by it﴾, he said: "Their minds will not be taken away."

Abu Ubayd said: "al-Akwab (the cups) are the abariq (pitchers) that have no spouts." Abu Ishaq said: "Its singular is kub (cup), which is a round vessel with no handle." Ibn Abbas said: "They are the abariq that have no ears (handles)." Muqatil said: "They are vessels with round heads and no handles." Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: "al-Akwab and al-abariq are those that have spouts." And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿There will circulate among them young boys of everlasting youth, with cups and pitchers and a cup from a flowing spring﴾.

The abariq are the akwab that have spouts. If they have neither spouts nor handles, they are akwab. Ibriq (pitcher) is on the pattern of ifil from al-bariq (sparkle), which is clarity; it is the vessel whose color gleams from its clarity. Then every vessel of its shape was called ibriq, even if it was not clear. The abariq of Paradise are of silver with the clarity of glass, so that what is within can be seen from its exterior. The Arabs call the sword ibriq because of the gleam of its color, and from it is the saying of Ibn Ahmar:

"I clung to a pitcher and clung to its sheath, so that it would destroy one who is living, of standing and of humble station."

In the Nawadir of al-Lihyani: "A woman is ibriq if she is radiant."

(Section)

As for al-kas (the cup), Abu Ubayda said: "It is the vessel together with what is in it."

Abu Ishaq said: "al-Kas is the vessel when there is wine in it, and the word kas applies to any vessel together with its drink."

The exegetes explained kas as wine, and this is the view of Ata, al-Kalbi and Muqatil, to the extent that al-Dahhak said: "Every kas in the Qur'an refers only to wine."

This is their consideration of the meaning and the intended sense, for what is intended is what is in the cup, not the vessel itself.

Also, some nouns are names both for the content and the container together and separately, such as nahr (river) and kas. For nahr is a name for the water and for its bed together, and for each of them individually. Likewise kas and qaryah (town), which is why the word qaryah is used to mean only its inhabitants, only its dwellings, or both together.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 56, verse 21:

[Section: On the Flesh of Birds]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the flesh of birds, of whatever they desire.﴾

In the Musnad of al-Bazzar and elsewhere, it is related with a raised chain (marfu'): "Indeed, you will look at a bird in Paradise and desire it, and it will fall roasted before you."

Some of it is lawful and some of it is unlawful. The unlawful is that which has talons (dhu al-mikhlab), such as the falcon, the hawk and the shahin; and that which feeds on carrion, such as the vulture, the nasr, the rakham, the laqlaq, the 'aqa'aq, the white-spotted crow and the large black crow; and that which it is forbidden to kill, such as the hoopoe and the surad; and that which it is commanded to kill, such as the kite and the crow.

The lawful kinds are many. Among them is the chicken. In the Two Sahihs, from the hadith of Abu Musa: "The Prophet (ﷺ) ate chicken meat."

It is hot and moist in the first degree, light on the stomach, quick to digest, good in its humours, increases the brain and semen, clarifies the voice, improves the complexion, strengthens the intellect, and produces good blood. It tends toward moisture. It is said that continual consumption of it causes gout (niqris), but this is not established.

The flesh of the rooster is hotter in temperament and less moist. The old rooster is a remedy that benefits colic (qawlanj), asthma (rabw) and thick wind, when boiled with the water of qurtum and dill (shibth). Its testicles are praiseworthy as food and quick to be digested. Chicks are quick to digest and laxative to the nature. The blood generated from them is fine and good.

Flesh of the durraj (partridge): hot and dry in the second degree, light and fine, quick to digest, produces balanced blood. Excess of it sharpens the sight.

Flesh of the hajal (chukar partridge): produces good blood and is quick to digest.

Flesh of the goose: hot and dry, poor as food when habitually eaten, and not very rich in excess humours.

Flesh of the duck: hot and moist, rich in excess humours, difficult to digest, and not agreeable to the stomach.

Flesh of the bustard (huban): In the Sunan, from the hadith of Buraydah ibn 'Umar ibn Safina, from his father, from his grandfather, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I ate bustard meat with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

It is hot and dry, difficult to digest, and beneficial for those who exercise and are tired.

Flesh of the crane (kurki): dry and light; its heat and coldness are disputed. It generates black bile (sawda'iyy) blood, suits those who labour and are weary, and it should be left for a day or two after slaughter before being eaten.

Flesh of sparrows and larks (qanabir): al-Nasa'i related in his Sunan, from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No person kills a sparrow or anything larger without its right, but Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, will question him about it." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah! What is its right?" He said: "You slaughter it and eat it, and do not cut off its head and throw it away."

Also in his Sunan, from 'Amr ibn al-Sharid, from his father, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever kills a sparrow in vain, it will cry out to Allah, saying: O Lord, so-and-so killed me in vain, and did not kill me for any benefit.'"

Its flesh is hot and dry, sharpens the nature, increases sexual potency; its broth softens the nature and benefits the joints. If its brains are eaten with ginger and onion, they arouse desire for intercourse; its mixing is not praiseworthy.

Flesh of pigeons: hot and moist; the wild ones are less moist, their young are more moist in quality, and those raised in houses and their young are lighter in flesh and more praiseworthy as food. The flesh of the males is a cure for paralysis, numbness, apoplexy and tremor; likewise smelling the breath of them, and eating their young helps with women, and it is good for the kidneys and increases blood. A hadith has been narrated about them which is false and has no basis from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "A man complained to him of loneliness, and he said: 'Take a mate from among the pigeons.'" A better narration than this is that he (ﷺ) "saw a man following a pigeon, and said: 'A devil following a she-devil.'"

'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, used to command, in his sermon, the killing of dogs and the slaughter of pigeons.

Flesh of the qata (sandgrouse): dry, generates black bile, constipates the nature, and is among the worst foods, except that it benefits dropsy (istisqa').

Flesh of the sumana (quail): hot and dry, benefits the joints, and harms the hot liver; its harm is averted with vinegar and kusfara. One should avoid the birds of marshes and foul places. The flesh of all birds is digested faster than that of livestock, and the quickest to digest are the least nourishing, namely the necks and wings; their brains are more praiseworthy than the brains of livestock.

Locusts: In the Two Sahihs, from 'Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa, who said: "We fought seven campaigns with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), eating locusts."

In the Musnad, from him: "Two dead animals and two bloods have been made lawful for us: fish and locusts, and liver and spleen." It is related both raised and as a statement of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.

It is hot and dry, of little nourishment; continual consumption of it causes emaciation. When fumigated with it, it benefits urinary retention and difficulty of urination, especially for women, and it is fumigated with it for hemorrhoids. Its fat is roasted and eaten for the sting of a scorpion. It is harmful to those with epilepsy and is of poor humour. Regarding the permissibility of its carcass dying without cause there are two opinions: the majority hold it lawful, while Malik prohibited it. There is no disagreement about the permissibility of its carcass if it dies from a cause, such as being crushed or burnt, and the like.

(Benefit)

A questioner asked: If Paradise has no death in it, how do they eat bird meat there, when it is an animal whose soul has departed?

It was answered that it is permissible that it not be dead.

This answer is

in extreme weakness.

Ibn 'Aqil said: "What compelled him to this, when Paradise is an abode in which no harm or fatigue is created at all? Rather, the eating is by way of honour, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, it is for you that you will not be hungry therein, nor will you be unclothed, and that you will not be thirsty therein, nor will you be exposed to the sun.﴾

And that is conditional upon obedience. If that is permissible regarding Adam, it is known that it is not obligatory regarding the bird, and it is not impossible in the power of Allah, the Exalted, that this bird be roasted, not from a soul that departed from it, or from a soul that departed outside Paradise and entered Paradise, while it is roasted meat."

I say: What necessitated all this contrivance?

Paradise is the abode of eternity for its people and inhabitants.

As for the bird, it is one kind of the foods which Allah creates for them, one after another; it is permanent in kind, though its individual units pass away, like fruit and other things.

And it has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that: "The believers will have sacrificed for them on the Day of Resurrection the bull of Paradise, which used to eat from it, so it will be their feast."

So this is an animal that used to eat from Paradise, and it is slaughtered as a feast for its people. And Allah knows best.

This is the commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 56, verses 25–26:

Regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿They will not hear therein any vain talk or sinful speech, but only the saying: "Peace, peace."﴾

In this there is a negation of hearing vain talk (laghw) and sinful speech (ta'thim), and an affirmation of their opposite, which is "peace" (salam), which contradicts both. Therefore the intended meaning is the negation of one thing and the affirmation of its opposite.

On this basis, there is no need to strain to make it fall under the excepted element (mustathna minhu), because that would eliminate this benefit of the statement.

Whoever refers it back to the first (interpretation) says: when He negated from them the hearing of vain talk and sinful speech, which are both things that are said, the soul became eager to know whether anything other than these would be heard therein, so He said: ﴿except the saying: "Peace, peace."﴾

Thus the meaning returns to: "They will not hear therein anything except the saying: 'Peace, peace.'"

When you reflect on these two interpretations, you will see that the first is more correct, for it negates the hearing of a thing and affirms its opposite.

Whereas on the second, it negates the hearing of everything except peace, and this is not the intended meaning, since they will hear peace and other things. So reflect upon it.

**Section: On the Trees of Paradise, Its Gardens and Its Shade**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And the companions of the right hand, what are the companions of the right hand? [They are] among lote trees without thorns, and banana trees layered with fruit, and extended shade, and water poured forth, and abundant fruit, neither cut off nor forbidden﴾.

And He says: ﴿Both having branches﴾, which is the plural of *fann*, meaning a branch (*ghusn*).

And He says: ﴿In both are fruit, palm trees, and pomegranates﴾.

*Al-makhdud* (المخضود) means that which has had its thorn removed (*khadda shawkatahu*), i.e., it has been stripped and cut off, so that there is no thorn on it.

This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Muqatil, Qatadah, Abu al-Ahwas, Qassamah ibn Zuhayr, and a group of others. These scholars argued with two proofs:

The first: *al-khadd* (الخضد) in the language means cutting. Every moist thing that you cut is *khadadtuhu*, and when you remove the thorn of a tree, it is *khadeed* and *makhdud*.

From this comes *al-khadd*, which is on the pattern of *ath-thamar*, and it is everything that is cut from a moist branch. *Makhdud* has the meaning of *khadeed*, like *qabd* and *salb*.

And *al-khadad* is a tree that is soft and has no thorns.

The second proof: Ibn Abi Dawud narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Musaffa narrated to us, Muhammad ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, Yahya ibn Hamzah narrated to us, Thawr ibn Yazid narrated to me, Habib ibn Ubayd narrated to me, from Utbah ibn Abd al-Sulami, who said: I was sitting with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when a Bedouin came and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I hear you mention in Paradise a tree, and I know of no tree with more thorns than it."

He meant the *talh* (طلح, a thorny acacia-type tree). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Indeed Allah has made in place of every thorn of it a fruit like the scrotum of a shorn male goat (*khasjwat al-taysi al-malbud*), in which there are seventy kinds of food, no one of which resembles another."

*Al-malbud* (الملبود) is the one whose hair has become matted, some of it upon other parts.

And Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said: Safwan ibn Amr informed us, from Sulaym ibn Amir, who said: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: "Indeed Allah benefits us through the Bedouins and their questions."

A Bedouin came one day and said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Allah has mentioned in Paradise a harmful tree, and I did not think there was in Paradise a tree that harms its companion." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "And what is it?" He said: "The *sidr* (lote tree), for it has a harmful thorn." He said: "Does not Allah say ﴿among lote trees without thorns﴾? Allah has removed the thorn and placed in place of every thorn a fruit."

Another group said: *al-makhdud* is the one laden with fruit (*al-mawqar hamlan*), and they denied this view, saying that *al-khadd* in the sense of "load" is not known in the language.

But those who denied this view were not correct; rather, it is a sound view, and its proponents held that when Allah, glory be to Him, removed a thorn and took it away, and placed in its place a fruit, the tree became laden with its load.

The two narrations mentioned combine the two views.

Similarly is the view of the one who said *al-makhdud* is that which does not wound the hand, and on which there is no thorn or harm that repels the hand.

He explained it by its *lazim al-ma'na* (necessary implication), and this is the practice of most commentators: they sometimes mention the necessary implication of the intended meaning, sometimes one of its instances, and sometimes one of its examples. Then those who gather all the good and the bad relate these as different opinions, though there is no real contradiction between them.

The second proof: Ibn Abi Dawud narrated to us: Muhammad ibn Musaffa narrated to us, Muhammad ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, Yahya ibn Hamzah narrated to us, Thawr ibn Yazid narrated to me, Habib ibn Ubayd narrated to me, from Utbah ibn Abd al-Sulami, who said: I was sitting with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when a Bedouin came and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I hear you mention in Paradise a tree, and I know of no tree with more thorns than it."

He meant the *talh* (طلح, a thorny acacia-type tree). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Indeed Allah has made in place of every thorn of it a fruit like the scrotum of a shorn male goat (*khasjwat al-taysi al-malbud*), in which there are seventy kinds of food, no one of which resembles another."

*Al-malbud* (الملبود) is the one whose hair has become matted, some of it upon other parts.

And Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said: Safwan ibn Amr informed us, from Sulaym ibn Amir, who said: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: "Indeed Allah benefits us through the Bedouins and their questions."

A Bedouin came one day and said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Allah has mentioned in Paradise a harmful tree, and I did not think there was in Paradise a tree that harms its companion." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "And what is it?" He said: "The *sidr* (lote tree), for it has a harmful thorn." He said: "Does not Allah say ﴿among lote trees without thorns﴾? Allah has removed the thorn and placed in place of every thorn a fruit."

Another group said: *al-makhdud* is the one laden with fruit (*al-mawqar hamlan*), and they denied this view, saying that *al-khadd* in the sense of "load" is not known in the language.

But those who denied this view were not correct; rather, it is a sound view, and its proponents held that when Allah, glory be to Him, removed a thorn and took it away, and placed in its place a fruit, the tree became laden with its load.

The two narrations mentioned combine the two views.

Similarly is the view of the one who said *al-makhdud* is that which does not wound the hand, and on which there is no thorn or harm that repels the hand.

He explained it by its *lazim al-ma'na* (necessary implication), and this is the practice of most commentators: they sometimes mention the necessary implication of the intended meaning, sometimes one of its instances, and sometimes one of its examples. Then those who gather all the good and the bad relate these as different opinions, though there is no real contradiction between them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 56, verse 29:

The majority of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: it is the banana (al-mawz). And al-mandud (the arranged, layered) is that which has been arranged one upon another, like a comb.

It was also said: al-talh is the thorny tree, whose every thorn has a fruit arranged in its place, so its fruit is arranged one upon another, and it is like the banana.

This latter view is more sound (asahh). The mention of the banana by the early scholars (al-salaf) was intended as an example (al-tamthil), not as a restriction (al-takhsis), and Allah knows best.

It is hot and moist. The best of it is the ripe and sweet. It benefits roughness of the chest, the lungs and coughing, and sores of the two kidneys and the bladder. It promotes urination, increases semen, stirs sexual desire for intercourse, loosens the bowels, and is eaten before meals. It harms the stomach, increases yellow bile (safra') and phlegm (balgham). Its harm is averted by sugar or honey.

(Section)

He said in (Hadi al-Arwah):

As for talh, most of the exegetes said it is the banana tree. Mujahid said: "The Arabs were impressed by talh wa-jh and it was beautified for them, so it was said to them: ﴿And talh arranged in tiers﴾."

This is also the view of Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. Another group said: rather, it is a large, tall tree, the tree of the desert (al-bawadi) that is abundant in thorns among the Arabs. Their caravan driver (hadi) said:

"Her guide gave her good news and said: 'Tomorrow you will see the talh and the mountains.'"

This tree has blossom, fragrance, and dense shade (zill zalil), and it has been arranged with fruit and produce in place of the thorns.

Ibn Qutaybah said: it is the one arranged with its fruit or its foliage, and the fruit runs from its base to its top, so it has no visible trunk.

Masruq said: the leaves of Paradise are arranged (nadid) from its bottom to its top, and its rivers flow without a trench.

Al-Layth said: talh is the tree of Umm Ghaylan. It has no thorn... it is the most curved of the great thorny trees, its roots are wood and its best is gum.

Abu Ishaq said: it is permissible that it means the tree of Umm Ghaylan, because it has a blossom of very pleasant fragrance, so they were addressed with it and promised what they love of its kind, except that its excellence over what is in this world is like the excellence of all that is in Paradise over all that is in this world, for in Paradise there is nothing but the names.

The apparent meaning is that whoever interpreted talh mandud as the banana intended only to give it as an example of beauty for the beauty of its arrangement; otherwise talh in the language is the large tree of the desert trees, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 56, verse 30:

In the two Sahihs, from the narration of Abu al-Zinad, from al-A'raj, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Indeed, in Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider can travel for a hundred years without crossing it. So recite, if you wish: ﴿And shade extended﴾."

And in the two Sahihs also, from the narration of Abu Hazim, from Sahl ibn Sa'd, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, in Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider can travel for a hundred years without crossing it." Abu Hazim said: "Then al-Nu'man ibn Abi 'Ayyash al-Zurqi narrated it to us, saying: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated to me from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'Indeed, in Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a swift, well-trained, fine riding horse can travel for a hundred years without crossing it.'"

Imam Ahmad said: Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from Abu al-Dahhak, who said: I heard Abu Hurayrah say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Indeed, in Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider travels for seventy or a hundred years. It is the tree of the Eternal Garden."

Waki' said: Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid narrated to us, from Ziyad, the freedman of Banu Makhzum, from al-Zuhri, from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Indeed, in Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider travels for a hundred years. Recite, if you wish: ﴿And shade extended﴾."

This reached Ka'b, and he said: "He spoke the truth, by Him who sent down the Torah upon the tongue of Musa and the Furqan upon the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ). If a man were to ride a young camel or a young ... and circle around the root of that tree for a hundred years, he would not reach it until he fell down in old age.

Allah planted it with His own hand and breathed into it. Its root is beyond the wall of Paradise, and there is no river in Paradise except that it flows out from the root of that tree."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: Ibrahim narrated to us, from Sa'id al-Jawhari, who said: Abu 'Amir al-'Aqadi narrated to us, saying: Rabi'ah ibn Salih narrated to us, from Salamah ibn Wahram, from Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said:

"(Extended shade) is a tree in Paradise on a trunk of such size that a swift, well-mounted rider could travel for a hundred years in its shade, in all its directions. The people of Paradise, the people of the lofty chambers, and others come out to it and converse in its shade.

Some of them desire and mention the pleasures of the world, so Allah sends a wind from Paradise, and that tree moves with every pleasure that existed in the world."

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, from the narration of Abu Hamid, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"There is no tree in Paradise except that its trunk is of gold."

He said: This is a hasan hadith. And from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, Allah says:

"I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. Recite, if you wish: ﴿No soul knows what is hidden for them of comfort for their eyes, as a reward for what they used to do﴾.

In Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider travels for a hundred years without crossing it. Recite, if you wish: ﴿And shade extended﴾.

And a place the size of a whip in Paradise is better than the world and what is in it. Recite, if you wish: ﴿So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has triumphed﴾."

Narrated with this wording and context by al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah.

Its beginning is in the two Sahihs. In Sahih al-Bukhari, from the narration of Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Indeed, in Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider can travel for a hundred years without crossing it. If you wish, recite: ﴿And shade extended, and water poured forth﴾."

Ibn Wahb said: 'Amr ibn al-Harith narrated to us, that Darraj Abu al-Samh narrated to him, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: A man said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), what is Tuba?" He (ﷺ) said:

"A tree in Paradise, a distance of a hundred years; the garments of the people of Paradise come out from its sheaths."

Harmalah narrated this from him with an addition, saying: Ibn Wahb informed me, 'Amr informed me that Darraj narrated to him that Abu al-Haytham narrated to him from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: A man said, "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Tuba to whoever saw you and believed in you!"

He said: "Tuba to whoever saw me and believed in me, then Tuba, then Tuba to whoever believed in me without seeing me."

A man said, "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), what is Tuba?"

He said: "A tree in Paradise, a distance of a hundred years; the garments of the people of Paradise come out from its sheaths."

I say: The beginning of this hadith is in the Musnad, and its wording is: "Tuba to whoever saw me and believed in me, and Tuba to whoever believed in me without seeing me," seven times.

Ibn al-Mubarak said: Sufyan narrated to us, from Hammad, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said:

"The palm trees of Paradise have trunks of green emerald, their crowns are red gold, their fronds are clothing for the people of Paradise, from which come their cloaks and garments, and their fruit is like large jars and buckets, whiter than milk, sweeter than honey, softer than butter, and without any pit."

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 56, verse 34:

Ibn Wahb said: Amr ibn al-Harith narrated to us from Darraj Abu al-Samah, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His words: ﴿And raised couches﴾

He said: "The distance between the two couches is like the distance between the heaven and the earth."

This is more likely to be the preserved (report). And Allah knows best.

Al-Tabarani said: Al-Miqdam ibn Dawud narrated to us, Asad ibn Musa narrated to us, Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from Ali ibn Zayd, from Mutarrif, from Abd Allah ibn al-Shakhkhir, from Ka'b concerning His words, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And raised couches﴾, he said: "A journey of forty years."

Al-Tabarani said: Ibrahim ibn Na'ilah narrated to us, Isma'il ibn Amr al-Bajali narrated to us, Israel narrated to us, from Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, from al-Qasim, from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about the raised couches, and he said: "If a couch were dropped from its highest point to its base, it would take a hundred years."

As for the raising (rafʿ, i.e. its attribution to the Prophet) of this hadith, there is doubt. Ibn Abi al-Dunya said: Ishaq ibn Isma'il narrated to us, Mu'adh ibn Hisham narrated to us, he said: I found in the book of Abu al-Qasim, from Abu Umamah, concerning His words, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And raised couches﴾, that he said:

"If its highest part fell, it would not reach its lowest part in forty autumns."

He returned the pronoun to the women, though no mention of them had preceded it, because the furnishings (al-furush) indicate them, since they are their place.

It has been said: the "furush" in His words ﴿and raised couches﴾ is a metaphor for the women, just as they are referred to by "the crystal-like ones" (al-qawarir), "the modest ones" (al-azr), and others. But His words "raised" (marfu'a) rule this out, unless it is said that what is meant is elevation of rank.

The Prophet's ﷺ explanation of the furush and their elevation has already been mentioned.

The correct view is that the furush are indeed the furnishings themselves, and they indicate the women because they are usually their place.

Qatadah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "We created them a new creation."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "He means the women of the human daughters."

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: "He means the women of the people of this world, the old women, white-haired."

God says: We created them after old age and decrepitude, after the first creation in this world.

Supporting this interpretation is the hadith of Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "They are your old women, bleary-eyed and rheumy-eyed."

It was narrated by al-Thawri from Musa ibn 'Ubayda from Yazid al-Raqqashi from him.

Also supporting it is what Yahya al-Hammani narrated: Ibn Idris told us from Layth from Mujahid from 'A'isha, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered upon her while there was an old woman with her.

He said: "Who is this?" She said: "One of my aunts." He said: "Indeed, no old woman will enter Paradise." Upon that the old woman was affected by what God willed. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed We have created them a creation anew" — they will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection barefoot, naked, uncircumcised; and the first to be clothed will be Ibrahim, the Friend of God. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: "Indeed We have created them a creation anew."

Adam ibn Abi Iyas said: Shayban told us from al-Zuhri from Jabir al-Ju'fi from Yazid ibn Murrah from Salamah ibn Yazid, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say concerning His words "Indeed We have created them a creation anew" — "meaning the married women and the virgins who were in this world."

Adam said: And al-Mubarak ibn Fudalah told us from al-Hasan, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The old woman shall not enter Paradise." So an old woman wept, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Inform her that on that day she will not be an old woman; she will be young. Indeed God, Mighty and Majestic, says: 'Indeed We have created them a creation anew.'"

Ibn Abi Shaybah said: Ahmad ibn Tariq told us, Mas'adah ibn al-Yasa' told us, Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah told us from Qatadah from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab from 'A'isha, that an old woman of the Ansar came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of God, pray to God that He admit me into Paradise." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, no old woman will enter Paradise." So the Prophet of God (ﷺ) left and prayed. Then he returned to 'A'isha, and 'A'isha said: "You have borne great hardship and distress from your words." He (ﷺ) said: "That is so. Indeed, when God Most High admits them into Paradise, He will transform them into virgins."

Muqatil mentioned another opinion, which is the view chosen by al-Zajjaj: that they are the houri (al-hur al-'in) mentioned earlier, whom God, Mighty and Majestic, created for His friends, and upon whom no childbirth has occurred.

The apparent meaning is that God created them in Paradise, a creation.

Several points indicate this:

First: He has said concerning the foremost (al-sabiqun): ﴿They will be attended by immortal youths, with cups...﴾ up to: ﴿like hidden pearls.﴾ He mentioned their lote-tree, their vessels, their drink, their fruit, their food, and their spouses, the houri. Then He mentioned the companions of the right hand, their food, their drink, their furnishings, and their women. The apparent meaning is that their women are like the women of those before them, created in Paradise.

Second: He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed We have created them a creation﴾, and this is apparently a first creation, not a second. For when He intends a second creation, He specifies it, as in His words: ﴿And that to your Lord is the final growth (al-nash'ah al-ukhra)﴾ and His words: ﴿And you have certainly known the first growth (al-nash'ah al-ula)﴾.

Third: the address in His words "and you were pairs, three kinds" onward is to males and females, and the second growth is likewise general to both kinds.

His words ﴿Indeed We have created them a creation﴾ apparently indicate that they are specific to this creation.

Consider His emphasis by the verbal noun (al-masdar).

The hadith does not indicate that the old women mentioned are specific to this attribute; rather, it indicates that they share with the houri these mentioned qualities.

So let it not be imagined that the houri are alone apart from them in what has been mentioned of qualities; rather, they are more deserving of it than they are. Thus the creation applies to both categories. And God knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 56, verse 37:

His saying: "ʿUruban" is the plural of ʿarūb (ʿarūb: a woman who is affectionate and loving toward her husband). They are the ones who make themselves beloved to their husbands.

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: ʿArūb among women is the one who obeys her husband and makes herself beloved to him.

Abu ʿUbayda said: ʿArūb is the good in tabbuʿ (tabaʿʿul: the good in being a wife, in attentiveness to her husband).

I say: He means her good accord with him and her gentleness toward her husband during intercourse.

Al-Mubarrad said: She is the one who is passionately in love with her husband.

He cited the verse of Labid:

"And in the litters are ʿurūb, not unchaste, / the hips of whom bring the eye to a dazzled halt."

The exegetes, in explaining "ʿuruban," said: they are the ʿawāsiq (ardently loving), the mutaḥabbibāt (those who make themselves beloved), the ghanjāt (coquettish), the shakkalāt (those who flirt with charm), the mutaʿashshiqāt (those who are passionately attached), the ghalimāt (ardent ones), and the maghnūjāt (playful, coy ones).

All of these are from their own vocabulary.

Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: "ʿUruban" with a heavy pronunciation, its singular is ʿarūb, like ṣabūr and ṣabr.

The people of Mecca call her al-ʿarabah, the people of Medina call her al-ghanjah, and the people of Iraq call her al-shakkalah. And the ʿurub are those who make themselves beloved to their husbands.

Thus he mentioned it in the Book of the Beginning of Creation.

In the Book of Tafsir, in the surah al-Waqiʿah, he said: "ʿUruban," heavy, that is, with the rāʾ vowelled with a ḍammah, its singular is ʿarūb, like ṣabūr and ṣabr.

The people of Mecca call her al-ʿarabah, the people of Medina call her al-ghanjah, and the people of Iraq call her al-shakkalah.

I say: He, glory be to Him, has combined in them the goodness of their appearance and the goodness of their companionship.

This is the utmost that is sought from women, and through it a man's pleasure with them is complete.

And in His saying: ﴿Neither man nor jinn has touched them before them﴾ is an indication of the perfection of pleasure with them.

For a man's pleasure with a woman whom no one else has had intercourse with has a superiority over his pleasure with another, and likewise it is with her as well.

He said in Rawdat al-Muhibbin:

As for ʿurub, it is the plural of ʿarūb, and she is the one who combines sweetness of appearance with goodness of conduct, attentiveness to her husband, making herself beloved to him by her speech, her conversation, the sweetness of her speech, and the goodness of her movements.

Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: As for atrab, it is the plural of tarib; it is said "so-and-so is the tarib of so-and-so" when the two are of the same age. They are equal in the age of youth, neither childhood has diminished them nor old age has aged them; rather their age is the age of youth. He, exalted is He, likened them to the hidden pearl, to the hidden eggs, and to the ruby and coral.

Take from the pearl the purity of its colour, the beauty of its whiteness and the softness of its texture; take from the hidden eggs, which are the protected ones that no hand has touched, the balance of their whiteness mixed with what beautifies them of a slight yellowness, unlike the chalky white that exceeds in whiteness; and take from the ruby and coral the beauty of their colour in their clarity and their tinge with a slight redness.

(Section)

So listen now to their description from the Truthful, the Believed (ﷺ). If the soul inclines and speaks to you of the proposal, well; otherwise, faith is defective. Muslim related in his Sahih, from the hadith of Ayyub, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: The men and the women in Paradise were being compared, whether they boasted or discussed, as to which are more numerous, and Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Did not Abu al-Qasim (ﷺ) say:

"The first company to enter Paradise will be in the form of the moon on the night of the full moon, and those after them in the light of a brilliant star in the sky, each man of them having two wives, the marrow of whose shins can be seen through the flesh, and there is no bachelor in Paradise."

Al-Tabarani said in his Mu'jam: Ahmad ibn Yahya al-Halwani and al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Qasawi narrated to us, saying: Sa'id ibn Sulayman narrated to us, from Fadl ibn Marzuq, from Abu Ishaq, from ʿAmr ibn Maymun, from ʿAbd Allah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said:

"The first company to enter Paradise will have faces like the moon on the night of the full moon. The second company will be upon the most beautiful brilliant star in the sky. Each one of them will have two wives from the dark-eyed houris, and upon each wife seventy garments, through which the marrow of their shins and their garments can be seen, just as red drink can be seen in a white glass."

The Hafiz Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Maqdisi said: This, in my view, is upon the condition of the Sahih.

In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Hammam ibn Munabbih, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"The first company to enter Paradise will have their forms upon the form of the moon on the night of the full moon. They will not spit in it, nor blow their noses in it, nor defecate in it. Their vessels and their combs are of gold and silver, their censers are of aloes wood, and their sweat is musk. Each one of them will have two wives, the marrow of whose shins can be seen through the flesh, because of their beauty. There will be no difference among them, nor any hatred; their hearts will be upon one heart. They will glorify Allah morning and evening."

Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal said in his Musnad: Yunus ibn Muhammad narrated to us, al-Khazraj ibn ʿUthman al-Sa'di narrated to us, Abu Ayyub, the freedman of ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan (may Allah be pleased with him), narrated to us, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"The space of a whip of one of you in Paradise is better than the world and all that is in it, and the bow-length of one of you in Paradise is better than the world and all that is in it, and a veil of a woman of Paradise is better than the world and all that is in it."

He said: I said, "O Abu Hurayrah, what is the veil?"

He said: "The head-covering. If this is the measure of the head-covering, what is the measure of the one who wears it!"

Ibn Wahb said: ʿAmr informed us that Darraj Abu al-Samh narrated to him, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"A man in Paradise will have a woman come to him who will strike upon his shoulders, and he will look at his face in her cheek, clearer than a mirror. And the least pearl upon her will light up what is between the east and the west. She will greet him with peace, he will return her greeting and ask her: Who are you? She will say: I am the one who is increased (al-Mazid). Upon her will be seventy garments, the least of which is like the al-Nuʿman (a fine cloth), and his sight will pass through them until he sees the marrow of her shin through all that. And upon them are crowns, and the least pearl upon them lights up what is between the east and the west."

Part of this hadith is in the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, and it is upon his condition.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"A morning or evening in the way of Allah is better than the world and all that is in it. The bow-length of one of you or the place of his whip (meaning his whip) is better than the world and all that is in it.

If a woman of the women of Paradise were to look down upon the earth, she would fill what is between them with fragrance and light up what is between them, and her veil upon her head is better than the world and all that is in it."

In the Musnad, from the hadith of Muhammad ibn Sirin, from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ):

"For the man of the people of Paradise are two wives from the dark-eyed houris, upon each of them seventy garments, through which the marrow of her shin can be seen."

Ibn Wahb said: ʿAmr narrated to us that Darraj Abu al-Samh narrated to him, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The lowest in rank among the people of Paradise is the one who has eighty thousand servants, seventy-two wives, and a dome of pearl, emerald and ruby is set up for him, as wide as the distance between al-Jabiyah and Sana'a." Narrated by al-Tirmidhi.

In the Mu'jam of al-Tabarani, from the hadith of Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The dark-eyed houris were created from saffron."

(Section)

In the Mu'jam of al-Tabarani: "That Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her) asked him, saying: O Messenger of Allah, inform me concerning the saying of the Exalted: ﴿ʿUruban atraban﴾ [al-Waqiʿah: 37]."

He said: "They are those who died in the world as old women, toothless with grey hair. Allah created them after old age and made them virgins, ʿurub (passionately loving), mutaʿashshiqat (ardently attached), mutaḥabbibat (making themselves beloved), atraban (of one age)."

I said: "O Messenger of Allah, are the women of this world better, or the dark-eyed houris?"

He said: "Rather, the women of this world are better than the dark-eyed houris, as the superiority of the outer garment over the lining."

I said: "O Messenger of Allah, and why is that?"

He said: "Because of their prayers, their fasting, and their worship of Allah, the Exalted. Allah clothes their faces in light and their bodies in silk, white of colour, green of garments, yellow of ornaments. Their censers are of pearl and their combs are of gold. They say: 'We are the everlasting, so we shall not die; we are the blessed, so we shall never be wretched; we are the ones who abide, so we shall never depart; we are the ones who are content, so we shall never be angry. Blessed is he for whom we are, and who is for us.'"

I said: "O Messenger of Allah, a woman among us marries two husbands, or three, or four, then dies and enters Paradise, and they enter with her. Which of them will be her husband?"

He said: "O Umm Salamah, she will be given the choice, and she will choose the best of them in character, and she will say: 'O Lord, this one was the best of them in character with me in the world, so marry me to him.' O Umm Salamah, the goodness of character has departed with the good of this world and the Hereafter."

He said in Rawdat al-Muhibbin:

He, glory be to Him, described them with His saying: ﴿Virgins, ʿurub, atraban﴾.

This is because of the excellence of having intercourse with a virgin, and its sweetness and delight over intercourse with a non-virgin. ʿĀ'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), if you passed by a tree from which animals had grazed and a tree from which none had grazed, in which would you let your camel graze?" He said: "In the one from which none had grazed." She meant that he had not married a virgin other than her.

And it is authentically reported from him that he said to Jabir when he married a non-virgin: "Why not a virgin, you could play with her and she with you?"

If it is said: This quality disappears with the first intercourse, so she becomes a non-virgin again?

It is said: The answer is from two angles.

The first: the purpose of intercourse with a virgin is that she has not tasted anyone before having intercourse with her, so his love is planted in her heart. That is more complete for the continuance of companionship. This is with respect to her.

As for with respect to the one who has intercourse with her, he is grazing a meadow which no one has grazed before him.

He, exalted is He, has indicated this meaning with His saying: ﴿Neither man nor jinn has touched them before them﴾.

Then after this, the pleasure of intercourse continues for him even when virginity has passed.

The second: it has been related that "the people of Paradise, whenever one of them has intercourse with a woman, she returns a virgin as she was, so whenever he comes to her he finds her a virgin."

(Exhortation)

If your lowly aspiration falls short of abandoning indecencies out of love for this Supreme Beloved, and you are not there, then abandon them out of love for the women whom Allah described in His Book and whom His Messenger (ﷺ) called to be united with in the Garden of Refuge. Some of their attributes and the pleasure of union with them have already been mentioned. If your aspiration falls short of them, and you are not worthy of proposing to them, and your soul calls you to prefer what is here over them, then be wary of His punishment, both immediate and deferred.

Know that punishments vary: sometimes they are hastened, sometimes deferred, and sometimes Allah combines both upon the sinner. The most severe punishment is the punishment of the removal of faith; below it is the punishment of the death of the heart and the erasure of the pleasure of remembrance, recitation, supplication and intimate conversation with Him. Sometimes the punishment of the heart creeps into it like the creeping of darkness, until the heart is filled with it and insight becomes blind. The lightest punishment is that which falls upon the body in this world, and lighter than it is what falls upon wealth. Sometimes the punishment of looking is in insight, or in sight, or in both.

Al-Fudayl said: Allah, the Exalted, says: "Son of Adam, when I turn you about in My blessings while you move about in My disobedience, beware lest I cast you down among your sins."

"Son of Adam, fear Me and sleep wherever you wish. If you remember Me, I will remember you; if you forget Me, I will forget you. And the hour in which you do not remember Me is against you, not for you."

Al-Fudayl also said: "What assures you that you have not openly defied Allah with an act for which He has detested you, so that He closes the doors of forgiveness upon you while you laugh?"

ʿAlqamah ibn Murthad said: While a man was circumambulating the House, a woman's forearm appeared to him, so he placed his forearm upon hers and took pleasure in it, and their forearms stuck together. He went to some of those elders, and they said: "Return to the place where you did this, and make a covenant with the Lord of the House that you will not return." He did so, and he was released.

(Section: On the fact that the majority of the people of Paradise are the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ)

In the two Sahihs, on the authority of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Prophet ﷺ said:

"Are you not content that you should be a quarter of the people of Paradise?" We said "Allahu akbar." Then he said: "Are you not content that you should be a third of the people of Paradise?" We said "Allahu akbar." Then he said: "I truly hope that you will be half of the people of Paradise. I will inform you about that: the Muslims among the disbelievers are only like a white hair on a black ox, or like a black hair on a white ox."

This is the wording of Muslim.

In al-Bukhari's version: "and like a black hair on a white ox, without the alif (i.e., ثور أبيض rather than أبيض with the definite form)."

From Buraydah ibn al-Husayb, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

"The people of Paradise are one hundred and twenty rows, and this Ummah makes up eighty of them."

Narrated by Imam Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, and its chain meets the conditions of the Sahih.

al-Tabarani narrated it in his Mu'jam from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abbas, and in its chain is Khalid ibn Yazid al-Bajali, concerning whom criticism has been made.

He also narrated it from the hadith of al-Qasim ibn Abd al-Rahman, from his father, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Prophet said:

"How will you be when a quarter of Paradise belongs to you and to the rest of people three quarters of it?"

They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best."

He said: "How will you be when a third of it [belongs to you]?"

They said: "That is more."

He said: "How will you be when half belongs to you?"

They said: "That is more."

Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The people of Paradise are one hundred and twenty rows, and of them, eighty rows are yours."

Al-Tabarani said: This hadith was not narrated from al-Qasim ibn Abd al-Rahman except by al-Harith ibn Khudayrah; Abd al-Wahid ibn Ziyad alone transmitted it.

Abdullah ibn Ahmad said: Musa ibn Ghaylan ibn Hashim ibn Makhlad narrated to us, from Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, from Sufyan, from Abu Amr, from his father, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: When the verse was revealed:

﴿A multitude from the earlier peoples (39) and a multitude from the later peoples (40)﴾

the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "You are a quarter of the people of Paradise; you are a third of the people of Paradise; you are half of the people of Paradise; you are two-thirds of the people of Paradise." Al-Tabarani said: Its raising to the Prophet was transmitted solely by Ibn al-Mubarak from al-Thawri.

Khaythamah ibn Sulayman al-Qurashi said: Abu Qilabah, namely Abd al-Malik ibn Muhammad ibn Bakkar al-Sayrafi, narrated to us, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Sufyan al-Thawri, from Bahz ibn Hakim, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said:

"The people of Paradise are one hundred and twenty rows, and you are eighty rows of them."

These hadiths have multiple routes and differing sources, and the chains of some are sound. There is no contradiction between them and the hadith of "half," because he first hoped that they would be half of the people of Paradise, so Allah granted him his hope and added to it another sixth.

Ahmad narrated in his Musnad, from the hadith of Abu al-Zubayr, that he heard Jabir say: I heard the Messenger of Allah say:

"I hope that those of my Ummah who follow me on the Day of Resurrection will be a quarter of the people of Paradise."

He said: "So we said Allahu akbar. Then he said: 'I hope that you will be half.'"

Its chain meets the conditions of Muslim.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 56, verse 57:

They did believe that He is their Creator, but He argued against them with their own creation, as proof of His oneness (tawhid, the affirmation of God's unity), of His knowledge, and of the truth of His messengers. He called them, through what He created in them and around them, to acknowledge His names and attributes, His oneness, the truth of His messengers, and belief in the return (ma'ad, the resurrection and final return to God).

He, glory be to Him, reminds His servants of His blessings upon them, and through these blessings He calls them to know Him, to love Him, to affirm His messengers, and to believe in meeting Him. This is what is contained in the surah of blessings, which is Surah al-Nahl, from His saying: ﴿He created man from a drop of fluid﴾ to His saying: ﴿And God has made for you shade from what He created, and has made for you refuges in the mountains, and has made for you garments that protect you from the heat, and garments that protect you from your violence. Thus He completes His favor upon you, that you might submit (to Him)﴾.

So He reminded them of the roots of the blessings and their branches, and enumerated them for them, one blessing after another. He informed them that He bestowed these blessings upon them so that they would submit to Him, and thus His blessings upon them would be completed through Islam, which is the head of all blessings.

(Section)

Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I have seen some physicians' statement in which they mentioned the cause of the variation in the duration of pregnancy, so I will mention it and mention what is in it.

He said: When the formation of the fetus is complete in a specific period, then if that period is increased by its equal, the fetus moves.

So if its double is added to the total, the fetus separates (is born).

He said: If its formation is complete in thirty days, then when it has sixty days, it moves. If the double of sixty is added to sixty, it becomes one hundred and eighty days, which is six months, and that is the period in which the pregnancy separates (ends in birth).

And if its formation is complete in thirty-five days, it moves at seventy, and separates at seven months.

And if its formation is complete at forty, it moves at eighty and separates at eight months.

And if it is complete at forty-five, it moves at ninety and separates at nine months, and so on by this calculation forever.

What this speaker mentioned requires the fetus to move before forty days, and this is definitely an error, for the spirit is only attached to it after the third forty days, and then it moves. Thus no movement is established for it before one hundred and twenty days. Whatever movement is estimated before that is not a self-originated, voluntary movement; rather it is perhaps an incidental movement caused by the membranes and fluids. The calculation he mentioned is supported by neither evidence nor consistent experience; it may exceed that or fall short of it. But what we are certain of is that the spirit is not attached to it except after the third forty days, and whatever movement is estimated before that, if it is authentic, was not caused by the spirit. And Allah knows best.

Consider His words, exalted is He, concerning the Event: ﴿Have you considered what you emit? Is it you who create it, or are We the Creator? We have decreed death among you﴾.

How He mentioned the beginning of the creation and its end, using them as evidence for the second creation, with His words ﴿And We are not to be outdone in replacing your likes and bringing you into being in what you do not know﴾. For you have only known the first creation in the wombs of your mothers, and its beginning is from what you emit. We will not be overcome in bringing you into a second creation in what you do not know. So you are like what you were in the world, in your forms and states. This is from the perfection of the power and will of the Lord, exalted is He. If you had remembered the conditions of the first creation, that would have guided you to the power of its Originator over the creation you denied. What argument and guidance is better than this, closer to reason and understanding, and further from every doubt and suspicion? Beyond this clarification and argument there is nothing but disbelief in God and in what the messengers brought, and belief.

He also said in (al-Tibyan fi Aqsam al-Qur'an):

His power over them has been announced, by which He may replace them with something better than them. In some places it is replacement by their likes, and in some it is His substituting a people other than them, who are then not like them. These are three matters whose points of agreement and difference must be known. Wherever replacement with something better than them occurs, it is an announcement of His power to remove them and bring others more obedient and more pious to Him in this world. This is His saying: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people, then they will not be like you﴾, meaning rather they will be better than you. Mujahid said: He replaces them with whomever He wills of His servants, making them better than these. They did not turn away, praise be to God, so He did not replace them.

As for His mention of the replacement of their likes, it is in Surat al-Waqi'ah and Surat al-Insan. In al-Waqi'ah He said: ﴿We have decreed death among you, and We are not to be outdone in replacing your likes and bringing you into being in what you do not know﴾.

In Surat al-Insan He said: ﴿We created them and strengthened their frames, and when We will, We replace their likes with a complete replacement﴾.

Many exegetes said: the meaning is that when We wish to create a creation other than you, no one precedes Us, and it does not escape Us.

In His words ﴿And when We will, We replace their likes with a complete replacement﴾: when We will, We destroy them and bring their counterparts, making them a replacement for them.

Al-Mahdawi said: a people agreeing with them in creation and differing from them in action.

Al-Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi did not mention any view other than this.

On this basis, these verses are like His saying: ﴿If He wills, He will remove you, O people, and bring others﴾. So it is an argument from His power to remove them and bring their likes, to His bringing them themselves when they die.

Then, exalted is He, argued from the first creation, reminding them of it, saying: ﴿And you have certainly known the first creation, so will you not remember?﴾ He alerted them, by what they knew and witnessed, to the truth of what His messengers told them about the second creation.

What I hold regarding the meaning of these two verses, the verse of al-Waqi'ah and the verse of al-Insan, is that the intended meaning of the replacement of their likes is the new creation and the final creation that they were promised.

Al-Zamakhshari was successful in understanding this from Surat al-Insan, when he said: "And We replaced their likes in the severity of their captivity," meaning the other creation.

Then he said: "It was also said: 'And We replaced others who obey,' and its proper form should be with 'in' (in) not 'when' (idha), like His saying: ﴿And if you turn away, He will replace you with another people﴾."

I say: His use of "idha" (when), which is used only for what is certain to occur, indicates the certain occurrence of this replacement, and that it will certainly happen. That is the other creation, whose possibility He argued for with His saying: ﴿And you have certainly known the first creation﴾.

He argued from the like to the like, and from what they witnessed and saw to what they denied. Their being like their likes is their being brought into a new creation of the very same kind: they are themselves in their very persons, and they are like themselves, so they are returned as themselves. If you say the resurrection is the very same as the first, you are right; and if you say it is like it, you are right too, for it is the same returned, or it is like the first. God, exalted is He, clarified this by His saying: ﴿Nay, they are in doubt about a new creation﴾.

So this new creation is what includes their being like their likes. God, exalted is He, called it a return (i'adah), and the return is like the origin; He called it another creation (nash'ah ukhra), which is like the first; He called it a new creation, which is like the first creation, as He said: ﴿Were We wearied by the first creation? Nay, they are in doubt about a new creation﴾; and He called them likes, while they are themselves. Thus the words of the Qur'an agree, each confirms the other, and each explains the other.

By this, objections raised by those who did not understand the resurrection that the messengers reported from God are dispelled. Nor do they understand from this statement what some later scholars said, that they are other than them in every respect.

This is certainly an error; God forbid that one should believe it. Rather, they are their likes, and they are themselves. When you understand the realities, no one disputes the expression except one of narrow outlook, small intellect, and weak knowledge.

(A Beneficial Principle)

From the moment the servant's foot settles in this abode, he is a traveler in it toward his Lord, and the duration of his journey is his life which has been decreed for him. Life is the duration of a person's journey in this abode toward God, exalted is He. Then days and nights have been made stages for his journey: every day and night is one of the stages. He continues traversing them stage after stage until the journey ends. The intelligent, discerning person is one who places each stage before his eyes, caring to cross it safe and gaining, and when he has crossed it, he places the next before his eyes. Time does not lengthen for him so that his heart hardens and his hope stretches, and he is caught up in procrastination, promises, delay and postponement. Rather, he counts his life as that single stage and strives to cross it with the best of what is before him, for when he is certain of its shortness and the speed of its passing, the work becomes easy for him, and his soul is brought to obey him in preparing provision. When he faces the next stage of his life, he faces it in the same way. He continues this practice until he traverses all the stages of his life, so his effort is praised and he rejoices in what he has prepared for the day of his need and want. When the dawn of the Hereafter rises and the darkness of this world clears, then he praises his night and his distress is lifted from him. How excellent is the one who meets his day when its dawn has broken and its success has become clear.

Then people in crossing these stages are of two kinds. One kind crosses them traveling toward the abode of wretchedness; every time they cross a stage, they draw nearer to that abode and farther from their Lord and from the abode of His honor. They cross those stages through what displeases the Lord, opposing His messengers, His allies and His religion, striving to extinguish His light, nullify His call, and establish a call other than it. These have their days made a journey to the abode for which they were created and employed. They are accompanied in it by the devils assigned to them, who drive them to their dwellings with driving, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have you not seen that We sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement?﴾ [Maryam: 83], meaning they provoke them, toward sins and disbelief with provocation, and drive them with driving.

The second kind crossed those stages traveling in them toward God and toward the abode of peace.

They are three kinds: one who wrongs himself, one who is moderate, and one who races to good deeds by God's permission.

All of these are prepared to journey and certain of the return to God, but they differ in gathering provision, packing it and choosing it, and in the journey itself, its speed and its slowness.

The one who wrongs himself falls short in provision, taking from it neither what suffices him to reach the destination, in quantity or quality; rather he is negligent with the provision he ought to take. Yet he gathers what harms him on the road, and finds the aftermath of its harm when he reaches the destination in proportion to what harmful thing he gathered.

The moderate one limits his provision to what suffices him, and does not load the packs of profitable trade, and does not take what harms him. He is safe and gaining, but he misses the profitable markets and the various noble gains.

The one who races to good deeds is concerned with obtaining profits and loading the packs of trade, knowing the measure of the gain that results. He sees it as a loss to keep anything in his hand without trading with it, so he finds his profit on the day when merchants rejoice in the profits of their trade. He is like a man who knows that ahead of him is a town where a dirham earns ten up to seven hundred and more, and who has capital and knows the road to that town and the skill of trade; if he could sell his clothes and everything he owns to prepare a trade to that town, he would do it. Thus is the state of the one who races to good deeds by his Lord's permission: he sees it as clear loss that any time should pass in which he is not trading.

**(Section: The Wisdom in Creating the Fire)**

They were given hair and wool that suffice them without it, and their nourishment was made of simple foods that need no cooking or baking. Since the need for fire is great, tools and means were created by which a person can kindle it when he wishes and extinguish it. Among its wisdoms are these lamps which people light, through which they accomplish many of their needs. As for its benefits in cooking foods and medicines and in warmth, these are not hidden.

These were singled out for mention because of their great need for it in baking and cooking, since they do not find anything they can buy that would spare them from making things by fire.

The point is that He, glory be to Him, made present in this abode what He has prepared for His friends and His enemies in the abode of permanence. He brought forth into this abode, from the traces of His mercy and His punishment, that which is a lesson and an indication of the good and evil there. He made these punishments, pains, trials and afflictions like whips by which He drives His believing servants.

When they see them, they are extremely cautious and infer from what they have seen and witnessed of them the disagreeable things and punishments of that abode. Their existence in this abode, their being shown to them, and their being tested with a small portion of them, was a mercy from Him toward them, a kindness to them, a reminder and an alert.

Since this abode has its good mixed with its evil, its harm with its comfort, and its delight with its torment, the wisdom of the Most Wise of the wise required that its good be separated from its evil, and that it be assigned to another abode, the abode of pure goodness and pure joy. Thus, the rule of mixing and blending was decreed upon this abode, and the two groups were intermingled in it. Some were tested by others, and some were made a trial for others. It is a perfect wisdom that dazzled minds, and an overpowering might.

Through this blending, the market of servitude was established as He loves and approves it. His servitude, which He loves and approves, could not be established except in this manner. Indeed, a single servant combines in himself the causes of good and evil, and one part of him is given power over another, so that He may extract from him the servitude He loves, which cannot be attained except thus. When the desired wisdom of this mixing and blending was achieved, He followed it with distinction and separation. He distinguished between the two through two abodes and two dwellings, assigned to each abode what suits it, housed in it those who suit it, and created believers who are God-fearing and sincere toward His mercy, and His enemies who are disbelievers deserving of His vengeance, and those who are sincere toward neither but are a mixture: these are the people of mercy, those are the people of vengeance, and these are the people of vengeance and mercy.

And there is another category that deserves neither reward nor punishment.

He arranged for each of these five categories its fitting ruling, and manifested in it His dazzling wisdom, so that His servants might know the perfection of His power and wisdom, that He creates what He wills, chooses from His creation whom He wills for choosing, that He places His reward in its proper place, and brings the two together in the place that befits that. He wrongs no one, nor does He diminish anything of anyone's right, nor does He punish anyone for other than his own offence.

This is in addition to the wisdoms inherent in this trial and testing that return to the servants themselves: the drawing out of their patience, gratitude, reliance on God and striving, and the bringing forth of the perfections latent in their souls from potency to act; the repelling of causes by one another, and the breaking of everything by confronting and colliding it with its opposite, so that the marks of subjugation, weakness and incapacity appear upon it, and the servant becomes certain that the Subduer (al-Qahhar) can only be One, and that it is impossible for Him to have a partner. Rather, subjugation and oneness are inseparable: sovereignty, power, strength and might all belong to God, the One, the Subduer, and whoever else is other than Him is a subject, subdued, having an opposite, a rival and a partner.

Thus He created the winds and gave some of them power over others, colliding with them, breaking their force and dispersing them. He created water and gave the winds power over it, turning and breaking it. He created fire and gave water power over it, breaking and extinguishing it. He created iron and gave fire power over it, melting it and breaking its strength. He created stones and gave iron power over them, breaking and crumbling them. He created Adam and his offspring and gave Iblis and his offspring power over them. He created Iblis and his offspring and gave the angels power over them, scattering them with every scattering and driving them with every driving. He created heat, cold, winter and summer, and gave each of them power over the other, removing and subduing it. He created night and day, and subdued each of them by the other. Likewise with animals of all their varieties, from land and sea, each has an opposite and an overcomer. Thus it became evident to minds and natures that the Subduer and Overcomer of all this is One, and that among the completeness of His dominion is the bringing into existence of the world in this manner: the binding of some of it to others, the making of some of it needy of others, the subduing of some by others, the testing of some by others, and the mixing of its good with its evil. He made its evil a ransom for its good. For this reason, on the Day of Resurrection, a disbeliever will be handed to every believer and it will be said to him: "This is your ransom from the Fire." Likewise, in this world, a believer is given power over trials, tests and calamities which become his ransom from the punishment of God. Those causes may also be a ransom for him from evils greater than them in this world. So let the intelligent person give this point its due reflection, and it will become clear to him the wisdom of the Subtle, the All-Aware.

Likewise, the wisdom in creating fire in the form it has, latent within its carrier, is that if it were manifest like air, water and earth, it would burn the world and everything in it. Since this supreme wisdom required this, animals were made self-sufficient without it in their clothing and their food. Since the need for fire is great, tools and means were created by which a person can kindle it when he wishes and extinguish it. Among its wisdoms are these lamps which people light, through which they accomplish many of their needs. Were it not for them, half of their lives would be like the lives of the people of the graves.

As for its benefits in cooking foods and medicines and in warmth, these are not hidden.
