**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 56, verse 74:**

The word composed of the letters zay, ya' and dal, for example, has a distinct, identifiable reality, so it deserves to be assigned a word that signifies it, because it is a thing that exists in the tongue and is heard by the ears. The word composed of hamzat al-wasl, sin and mim (ism, "name") is an expression for the word composed of zay, ya' and dal, for example.

The word composed of zay, ya' and dal is an expression for the person who exists in external reality and in minds.

This (person) is the *musamma* (the named thing) and the meaning. The word that signifies it, which is zay, ya' and dal, is the *ism* (name).

This word has also become a *musamma*, insofar as the word hamza, sin and mim is an expression for it.

It has thus become clear to you that the *ism* (name), in its original imposition, is not the *musamma* (the named thing). That is why you say: "I named this person with this name," just as you say: "I adorned him with this adornment (*hilya*)."

The adornment is other than the one adorned, and likewise the name is other than the named thing.

Sibawayh explicitly stated this. Whoever attributed to him something other than this has erred, and claimed that his position is the identity of the two.

What misled the one who made that claim is his statement: "The verbs are patterns (*amthila*), taken from the forms of the nouns' events."

But this does not contradict his explicit statement before it, for he stated that the name is other than the named thing.

He said: "The words (*kalim*) are *ism*, *fi'l* (verb) and *harf* (particle)." He thereby explicitly declared that the *ism* is a word. How then could the word be the named thing, when the named thing is a person? Then he said after this: "You say, 'I named Zayd with this name,' just as you say, 'I marked him with this sign.'"

In his book, in nearly a thousand places, he says that the *ism* is the word that signifies the named thing. Whenever he mentions the genitive (*khafd*), the accusative (*nasb*), the nunation (*tanwin*), the definite article (*lam*), or everything that attaches to the *ism* by addition or subtraction, diminutive or augmentative forms, *i'rab* (grammatical inflection) or *bina'* (indeclinability), all of that is among the accidents of the *ism*, and has no connection at all to the named thing.

No grammarian or Arab ever said that the *ism* is the named thing.

They say: "The appointed term (*ajal musamma*)," and do not say "ajal ism." They say: "The *musamma* of this name is such-and-such."

No one says: "The *ism* of this *ism*." They say: "This is named (*musamma*) Zayd," and they do not say: "This man is the *ism* of Zayd."

They say: "In the name of Allah (*bi-ismi Allah*)," and do not say: "In the named thing of Allah (*bi-musammā Allah*)."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I have five names (*li khamsatu asma'*)."

It is not correct to say: "I have five named things (*khams musammayat*)."

He said: "Name yourselves by my name (*fa-tasammaw bi-ismi*)."

It is not correct to say: "Name yourselves by my named things (*bi-musammayati*)."

He said: "Allah has ninety-nine names (*li-Allahi tis'atun wa-tis'una ismān*)."

It is not correct to say: "Allah has ninety-nine named things (*musamma*)."

When the difference between the *ism* and the *musamma* has become evident, there remains here the *tasmiya* (naming). It is this that the one who holds the identity of the name and the named thing took into account. The *tasmiya* is an expression for the act of the one who names, and his placing the name upon the named thing, just as *tahliya* (adorning) is an expression for the act of the one who adorns, and his placing the adornment upon the one adorned.

Thus there are three realities here: *ism* and *musamma* and *tasmiya*, like *hilya*, *muhallā* (the adorned) and *tahliya*; and *'alama* (sign), *mu'allam* (the one marked), and *ta'lim* (marking).

There is no way to make two of these synonymous with one meaning, because their realities are distinct. And if you make the *ism* the same as the *musamma*, one of these three realities is necessarily nullified.

If it is said: "Then solve for us the doubt of the one who holds their identity, so that the proof is complete. For you have established the proof, so it is incumbent on you to answer the objection."

Among them is the claim that Allah alone is the Creator, and whatever else is created. So if His names were other than Him, they would be created. It would follow that He had no name or attribute in eternity, because His names are attributes.

This is the greatest question, which led the affirmers of attributes (*mutakallimu al-ithbat*) to say: "The *ism* is the *musamma*." So what do you have to repel it?

The answer: The source of error in this topic is the use of a term that is ambiguous between two meanings, one correct and one false. The dispute is not resolved except by distinguishing those meanings and applying their expressions to them. There is no doubt that Allah, blessed and exalted, has always been and always will be described by the attributes of perfection from which His names are derived. He has always been, with His names and attributes, one Lord and one God, to whom belong the most beautiful names and the sublime attributes. His names and attributes are included in the *musamma* of His name, although the attribute is not itself called "God who creates and provides." So His attributes and names are not other than Him, nor are they the very essence of God. The people's affliction comes from the word "other" (*al-ghayr*), which is used for two meanings.

One: that which differs from that essence named "Allah." Whatever differs from Allah with absolute difference in this sense is nothing but created.

The other: the difference of the essence when something is separated from it.

So when it is said: "The knowledge of Allah and the speech of Allah are other than Him," meaning that they are other than the essence stripped of knowledge and speech, the meaning is correct. But the expression is false.

And if knowledge and speech were different from His particular reality by which He is distinguished from others, the statement would be false in wording and meaning.

With this, the People of the Sunnah answered the Mu'tazila who held that the Qur'an is created, and they said: "His speech, exalted is He, is included in the *musamma* of His name."

So "Allah" is a name for the essence described by the attributes of perfection. Among those attributes is the attribute of speech, just as His knowledge, power, life, hearing and sight are uncreated. And since the Qur'an is His speech, and it is one of His attributes, it includes His most beautiful names.

If the Qur'an is uncreated, and it is not said that it is other than Allah, then how can it be said that some of what it includes, namely His names, are created and other than Him?

Thus the truth has become manifest, by the praise of Allah, and the doubt has been resolved: His most beautiful names that are in the Qur'an are from His speech, and His speech is uncreated.

It is not said that it is other than Him, nor that it is He.

This position differs from the position of the Mu'tazila, who say that His names, exalted is He, are other than Him and are created, and from the position of those who refuted them, who say: "His name is the very essence of Him, not other than Him."

With the detailed explanation, doubts disappear and the correct view becomes clear, praise be to Allah.

A second argument for them: They said: Allah, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord﴾, and ﴿Mention the name of your Lord﴾, and ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾.

This argument is against them, not for them, in reality. For the Prophet ﷺ acted upon this command, and said: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High (*subhana rabbiya al-a'la*). Glory be to my Lord, the Mighty (*subhana rabbiya al-'azim*)."

If the matter were as they claim, he would have said: "Glory be to the name of my Lord, the Mighty."

Furthermore, none of the Muslim community may say: "I worshipped the name of my Lord," or "I prostrated to the name of my Lord," or "I bowed to the name of my Lord," or "The name of my Lord, have mercy on me." This shows that acts are connected to the named thing, not to the name.

As for the answer to the connection of the remembrance and glorification commanded with "name": it has been said that when exaltation and transcendence are due to the one exalted, one may exalt what is from his cause and connected to him, as one says: "Peace upon the lofty presence, the exalted gate, the noble assembly," and similar expressions. But this answer is unsatisfactory for two reasons.

One: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not understand this meaning. He said "Glory be to my Lord," and did not turn to what you mentioned.

Two: it would require that one attribute to the name the magnification, praise, and declaration of the oneness of God that are attributed to the named thing, so that one would say: "Praise belongs to the name of Allah," and "There is no god but the name of Allah," and similar. Yet no one has said this.

Rather, the correct answer is this: true remembrance (*dhikr*) is primarily in the heart, because it is the opposite of forgetfulness. Glorification (*tasbih*) is a kind of remembrance. So if remembrance and glorification are mentioned without qualification, one understands from them only that, not merely the utterance with the tongue. Yet Allah wills both from His servants together, and He does not accept faith or the bond of Islam except with the conjunction and union of both.

So the meaning of the two verses becomes: Glorify your Lord with your heart and your tongue; remember your Lord with your heart and your tongue. The word "name" was inserted to alert to this meaning, so that remembrance and glorification are not free of utterance by the tongue. For the remembrance of the heart has as its object the named thing indicated by the name, and nothing else. But remembrance by the tongue has as its object the word together with what it signifies, because the word is not intended for itself. So no one should imagine that the word is what is glorified, apart from the meaning it indicates.

My shaykh Abu al-'Abbas Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah sanctify his soul, expressed this meaning to me in a concise and subtle phrase. He said: "The meaning is: glorify, uttering with speech and speaking by the name of your Lord."

Likewise, "glorify the name of your Lord" means: glorify your Lord while mentioning His name.

This benefit is worth a journey, but only for one who knows its value. So praise be to Allah, the Bestower, by His grace, and we ask Him to complete His favor.

A third argument for them: They said: Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿You worship besides Him nothing but names that you have named﴾, and they only worshipped what they named.

The answer: as you said, they only worshipped the named things, but because they gave them false names, like al-Lat and al-'Uzza. These are mere false, untrue names with no named reality in fact. For they named them gods and worshipped them, believing in the reality of divinity for them.

Yet they have nothing of divinity except bare names, not the reality of the named thing.

So they worshipped nothing but names that have no realities for their named things.

This is like one who named onion skins "meat" and ate them. It is said to him: "You ate nothing of meat but its name, not its named thing."

And like one who named dirt "bread" and ate it. It is said: "You ate nothing but the name of bread." Indeed, this negation is more forceful in negating the divinity of their gods.

For there is no reality of divinity for them in any way, and there is nothing there but a bare name.

So reflect on this noble benefit in the speech of Allah, exalted is He.

If it is asked: What is the purpose of the particle *bi* (in) in His saying: ﴿So glorify with the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾, while it does not occur in His saying: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾?

It is answered: *Tasbih* is intended as transcendence and bare remembrance, without any other meaning. It is also intended, together with that, as prayer, which is remembrance and transcendence with action.

That is why prayer is called *tasbih*.

When bare glorification is intended, there is no meaning for *bi*, because it is not transitive by a preposition. You do not say: "I glorified with Allah."

When what is combined with action, namely prayer, is intended, you add *bi*, as an alert to that intended meaning, as if you said: "Glorify, beginning with the name of your Lord," or "speaking with the name of your Lord." Just as you say: "Pray, beginning," or "speaking his name." For this secret, and Allah knows best, the preposition *li* (for) entered in His saying: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah﴾.

The intended glorification is that of prostration, submission and obedience. He did not say in any place: "Glorify Allah, whatever is in the heavens and the earth," just as He said: ﴿And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾.

And reflect on His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are near your Lord do not disdain to worship Him, and they glorify Him, and to Him they prostrate﴾.

How He said "and they glorify Him" after mentioning prostration by its specific name: so glorification became their remembrance of Him and their declaring Him free of imperfection.

(Fā'idah)

Since the purpose of this oath is to negate what the disbelievers said about the Qur'an, namely that it is poetry, or soothsaying, or "the fables of the ancients," the statement was introduced with the particle of negation, and then what they claimed was affirmed for it. Thus the verse contains: the matter is not as they allege, but rather it is a Noble Qur'an.

For this reason, both things were stated explicitly: the negation and the affirmation.

(Faṣl)

Among this is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars. And indeed it is an oath, if you only knew, a tremendous one. Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an, in a Book well-guarded, which none touches except the purified. A revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾

He, glorified is He, mentioned this oath after mentioning the Great Resurrection and the divisions of creation therein. Then He mentioned the decisive proofs of His power and of the Return through the first creation, the bringing forth of plants from the earth, the sending down of water from the sky, and the creation of fire. Then after that He mentioned the states of people at the Lesser Resurrection, at the separation of the soul from the body. He swore by the positions of the stars to establish the firmness of the Qur'an and that it is a revelation from Him.

There has been disagreement concerning the stars by whose positions He swore. It was said: they are the verses of the Qur'an, and their "positions" are their descent, one piece after another.

This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, in the narration of 'Ata', and the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Qatadah.

It was said: the stars are the planets, and their "positions" are their setting places at sunset.

This is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah and others.

It was said: their "positions" are their scattering and their dimming on the Day of Resurrection.

This is the view of al-Hasan.

Among the arguments for this view is that the word (mawāqi') implies it, for it is a form of mafā'il from al-wuqū' (falling), which is descent, so every star has a position (mawqi'), and its plural is mawāqi'.

This view is also strengthened by the fact that wherever "stars" (nujūm) occurs in the Qur'an, what is meant by it is the planets, as in His saying: ﴿And the retreat of the stars﴾, and His saying: ﴿The sun and the moon and the stars﴾.

Verbal nouns, when their types differ, are put in the plural, and when the type is one, they are put in the singular. Thus the singular "mawqi'" is for the unity of what is annexed to it, and the plurality of "mawāqi'" is for its plurality, since every star has a position.

(Fā'idah)

Since the purpose of this oath is to negate what the disbelievers said about the Qur'an, namely that it is poetry, or soothsaying, or "the fables of the ancients," the statement was introduced with the particle of negation, and then what they claimed was affirmed for it. Thus the verse contains: the matter is not as they allege, but rather it is a Noble Qur'an.

For this reason, both things were stated explicitly: the negation and the affirmation.

Among this is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars. And indeed it is an oath, if you only knew, a tremendous one. Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an, in a Book well-guarded, which none touches except the purified. A revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾

He, glorified is He, mentioned this oath after mentioning the Great Resurrection and the divisions of creation therein. Then He mentioned the decisive proofs of His power and of the Return through the first creation, the bringing forth of plants from the earth, the sending down of water from the sky, and the creation of fire. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, in the narration of 'Ata', and the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Qatadah.

This is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah and others.

(Section)

The matter sworn to here is His saying ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾.

An interjection came between the oath and its response with His saying ﴿And indeed it is a great oath, if you only knew﴾. Within this interjection another interjection came between the attribute and the thing described, in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿if you only knew﴾. This interjection within an interjection is the most delicate and the most excellent in its placement. An interjection is at its best when it carries emphasis, an alert, or a safeguard, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds—We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity; those are the companions of Paradise, therein they will abide forever﴾.

So He interjected between the subject and the predicate with ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾, because it contains a safeguard that repels the assumption of one who might think that the promise is owed only to one who has brought all the righteous deeds; so this was removed by ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾.

This is better than the view of those who said that it is a predicate about "those who believe," and then a second predicate was given about them, so that they would be two predicates about one subject. For the absence of burdening beyond capacity is not specific to those who believe; it is a ruling that encompasses all creation. Moreover, that assumption leaves the predicate without a connecting pronoun, requires positing a deleted attribute (i.e., "a soul from among them"), and nullifies this great benefit.

(Section)

Then He said ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾, describing it with what requires its goodness, the abundance of its good and its benefits, and its greatness. Al-karīm (noble) is that which is radiant, abundant in good, and great in benefit, and it is, of every thing, the best and most excellent of it. Allah, glorified is He, described Himself as noble (karīm), described His speech with it, described His Throne with it, and described with it that which abounds in good and is pleasant to behold, such as plants and other things. For this reason the early scholars (al-salaf) explained karīm as "good." Al-Kalbī said: "Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an" means "good, noble before Allah." Muqātil said: "Allah ennobled it and made it honored, because it is His speech." Al-Azharī said: "Al-karīm is a comprehensive term for what is praised, and Allah is karīm, beautiful in His acts. And indeed it is a noble Qur'an, praised for the guidance, clarity, knowledge, and wisdom in it."

In sum, the karīm is one who by nature gives much good with ease and facility, and its opposite is the lāʾim (base, ignoble), who does not bring forth even a little of his good except with difficulty and hardship. Likewise, the karīm among people and the lāʾim.

(Section)

Then He, exalted is He, said ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾.

The exegetes differed regarding this. It was said that it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ). The correct view is that it is the Book that is in the hands of the angels, which is the one mentioned in His saying ﴿in honored scrolls, exalted, purified, in the hands of scribes, noble and obedient﴾.

What shows that it is the Book in the hands of the angels is His saying ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾. This indicates that it is in their hands, and they touch it. This is the correct meaning of the verse. Among the exegetes is one who said that what is meant is that the muṣḥaf (the codex) is touched only by one who is in a state of purity.

The first view is more likely, for several reasons:

First: the verse was brought to declare the Qur'an free from being brought down by the devils, and that its place—none touches it except the purified. It is impossible for the most wicked and impure of Allah's creatures to reach it or touch it, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The devils did not bring it down, nor is it befitting for them, nor are they able to.﴾ He negated the act, its being fitting for them, and their ability to do it. They did not do it, it is not fitting for them, and they are not able to. For an act may be negated from one who would be capable of it, and may be fitting for one who is not able to do it. So He negated these three matters from them. Likewise His saying in Surat ʿAbasa: ﴿in honored scrolls, exalted, purified, in the hands of scribes, noble and obedient﴾. He described its place with these attributes, making clear that the devil cannot approach it.

The explanation of this meaning is more important, more beautiful, and more beneficial than explaining that the muṣḥaf is not touched except by the pure.

The second aspect: the surah is Meccan, and in Meccan surahs the concern is with the foundations of religion: establishing tawḥīd, the resurrection, and prophethood. Establishing rulings and laws is the domain of the Medinan surahs.

The third: the Qur'an was not in a codex (muṣḥaf) at the time this verse was revealed, nor in the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; it was gathered into a codex in the caliphate of Abū Bakr. Even if it is permissible that this be taken as a consideration of what will come, the apparent meaning is that it is a report of the present reality, which clarifies it.

The fourth: His saying "in a Book well-guarded." The maknūn is the preserved, hidden from eyes, that which the hand of man cannot reach, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿as if they were hidden eggs﴾. The early scholars said likewise. Al-Kalbī said: "maknūn: protected from the devils." Muqātil said: "hidden." Mujāhid said: "no dust or dirt touches it." Abū Isḥāq said: "preserved in the heaven." This clarifies it.

The fifth: describing it as maknūn is parallel to describing it as maḥfūẓ (preserved). So His saying ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an, in a Book well-guarded﴾ is like His saying ﴿Rather, it is a glorious Qur'an, in a Preserved Tablet﴾. This clarifies it.

The sixth: this is more conclusive in refuting the deniers, and more emphatic in exalting the Qur'an, than saying the muṣḥaf is not touched by one in a state of minor impurity.

The seventh: His saying ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾ is in the nominative (marfūʿ), so it is a predicate both in wording and meaning. Had it been a prohibition, it would have been in the jussive/with a fatḥa. Whoever takes the verse as a prohibition must turn the predicate away from its apparent sense to the meaning of a prohibition, and the basic principle is that both report and prohibition are kept to their literal sense; there is no reason here that compels turning the statement from report to prohibition.

The eighth: He said "al-muṭahharūn" (the purified) and did not say "al-mutaṭahharūn" (those who purify themselves). Had He meant to forbid touching it to one in a state of minor impurity, He would have said "al-mutaṭahharūn," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves﴾.

In a hadith: "O Allah, make me among the constantly repentant, and make me among those who purify themselves."

The one who purifies himself (mutaṭahhir) is the doer of purification, and the muṭahhar is one whom another has purified. So the one performing ablution is mutaṭahhir, and the angels are muṭahharūn.

The ninth: if what was meant were the codex in our hands, there would be little benefit in reporting that it is maknūn. For mere being spoken in a book does not entail its being preserved. How then would the Qur'an be praised for being maknūn in a book? This is a common matter, whereas the verse was brought to state its praise and honor, and the distinctive qualities that show it was sent down from Allah, and that it is protected and guaranteed, that no devil reaches it in any way, and that none touches its place except the purified, who are the noble, obedient scribes.

The tenth: what Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr related in his Sunan: Abū al-Aḥwaṣ narrated to us, ʿĀṣim al-Aḥwal narrated to us, from Anas ibn Mālik regarding His saying ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾: he said, "The purified are the angels."

This, according to a group of the people of hadith, has the ruling of the attributed-to-the-Prophet (marfūʿ). Al-Ḥākim said: "The tafsīr of the Companions is, according to us, in the ruling of the marfūʿ." And whoever does not make it marfūʿ, there is no doubt that it is, in his view, more authentic than the tafsīr of those after the Companions, and the Companions are the most knowledgeable of the Ummah in the tafsir of the Qur'an, and it is obligatory to return to their explanation. Ḥarb said in his Masāʾil: "I heard Isḥāq regarding His saying ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾: he said, 'The copy that is in heaven—none touches it except the purified,' he said, 'the angels.'"

I heard Shaykh al-Islām establish the argument from the verse for the view that the muṣḥaf is not touched by one in a state of minor impurity, in another way. He said: "This is from the category of alerting and indication: if those scrolls in heaven are touched only by the purified, then the scrolls of the Qur'an in our hands ought likewise not to be touched except by one who is pure." And the hadith is derived from this verse.

And His saying (in the hadith): "None touches the Qur'an except one who is pure." It was related by the people of the Sunan from the narration of al-Zuhrī, from Bakr ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm, from his father, from his grandfather, that in the document which the Prophet ﷺ wrote to the people of Yemen concerning the Sunan, the obligatory shares, and the blood-money:

"That none touches the Qur'an except one who is pure."

Aḥmad said: "I hope that it is authentic." And he also said: "I have no doubt that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wrote it." Abū ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Barr said: "It is a well-known document among the people of biography and known among the people of knowledge with a knowledge that is sufficient by its fame without an isnād, because its transmission resembles mass-transmission (tawātur) in the way people received it with acceptance and recognition." Then he said: "It is a document known among the scholars, and what is in it is agreed upon, except a little. It was related by Ibn Ḥibbān in his Ṣaḥīḥ and by Mālik in his Muwaṭṭaʾ." There are other reports on this issue, mentioned in other places.

(Section)

The verse, by its indication and allusion, shows that its meanings are not grasped nor understood except by pure hearts. It is forbidden for a heart soiled with the impurity of innovations (bidaʿ) and violations to attain its meanings or to understand it as it should be understood. Al-Bukhārī said in his Ṣaḥīḥ regarding this verse: "None finds its taste except one who believes in it." This too is from the allusion and alert of the verse: that none delights in it, in its recitation, its understanding, and its reflection, except one who bears witness that it is the speech of Allah, spoken by Him truly, and sent down to His Messenger as revelation. And none attains its meanings except one in whose heart there is no discomfort with it in any respect. Whoever does not believe that it is true from Allah has discomfort with it in his heart. Whoever does not believe that Allah, exalted is He, spoke it as revelation, and that it is not a created thing among His creation, has discomfort with it in his heart. Whoever says it has an inner meaning contrary to its outer meaning, and that it has an interpretation contrary to what is understood from it, has discomfort with it in his heart. Whoever says it has an interpretation that we do not understand or know, and that we only recite it, worshipping through its words, has discomfort with it in his heart. Whoever subjects it to the speculations of the rationalists, the nonsense of the theologians, the sophistry of the sophists, or the fancies of the Sufis, has discomfort with it in his heart. Whoever makes it subordinate to his sect, his school, and the sayings of the one he follows in religion, bending it to his sayings and laboring to force it onto them, has discomfort with it in his heart. Whoever does not make it the judge, outwardly and inwardly, in the foundations and branches of religion, and does not submit and yield to its judgment wherever he is, has discomfort with it in his heart.

Whoever is not commanded by its commands, does not refrain from its prohibitions, does not affirm all its reports, does not subordinate his command, prohibition, and report to it, and does not reject every command, prohibition, and report that contradicts it, has discomfort with it in his heart. All of these have had their hearts not touched by its meanings, and they do not understand it as it should be understood, and they do not find of its sweetness and taste what the Companions and those who followed them found.

If you reflect on His saying ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾, and give the verse its due from the indication of its wording, its allusion, its hint, its alert, the analogy of a thing to its like, and its consideration through its similarities, and you reflect on the correspondence which Allah, glorified is He, established and linked between the outer and the inner, you will understand all these meanings from the verse. And success is from Allah.

(Section)

And if you reflect on His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an (77), in a Book well-guarded (78), none touches it except the purified (79)﴾

you will find the verse to be among the clearest proofs of the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ, that this Qur'an came from Allah, and that the one who brought it is a purified spirit, so the wicked spirits have no path to it. You will find the verse the sister of His saying: ﴿And the devils did not bring it down (210), nor is it befitting for them, nor are they able [to]﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 211].

You will find it indicating, in the best indication, that none touches the muṣḥaf except one who is pure. And you will find it indicating also, in the most subtle indication, that none finds its sweetness and taste except one who believes in it and acts by it, as al-Bukhārī understood from the verse, and said in his Ṣaḥīḥ, in the chapter: ﴿Say: bring the Torah and recite it﴾: "None touches it" means none finds its taste and benefit except one who believes in the Qur'an, and none carries it rightfully except a believer, based on His saying: ﴿The likeness of those who were entrusted with the Torah, then did not bear it, is like a donkey carrying books﴾ [al-Jumuʿa: 5].

You will also find underneath it that none attains its meanings and understands it as it should be understood except pure hearts, and that impure hearts are prevented from understanding it and turned away from it. So reflect on this close kinship and the bond of brotherhood between these meanings and the apparent meaning of the verse, and the deriving of all these meanings from the verse in the best and clearest way.

﴿None touches it except the purified (79)﴾

(Section)

Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah said:

The correct view regarding the verse is that what is meant by it is the scrolls that are in the hands of the angels, for several reasons.

Among them: He described it as maknūn, and the maknūn is that which is hidden from eyes. This applies only to the scrolls that are in the hands of the angels.

Among them: He said ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa: 79], and they are the angels. Had He meant those who are in a state of ablution, He would have said: "None touches it except those who purify themselves," as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Baqara: 222]. So the angels are muṭahharūn (purified), and the believers are mutaṭahhirūn (those who purify themselves).

Among them: this is a report. Had it been a prohibition, it would have been "lā yamassuhu" with a jussive. The basic principle of a report is that it is a report in form and in meaning.

Among them: this is a refutation of one who said that the devil brought this Qur'an. So He, exalted is He, reported that it is in a Book well-guarded, which the devils do not reach; there is no way for them to it, as He, exalted is He, said in the verse of al-Shuʿarāʾ: ﴿And the devils did not bring it down, nor is it befitting for them, nor are they able [to]﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 210–211]. Only the purified spirits reach it, and they are the angels.

Among them: this is parallel to the verse in Surat ʿAbasa: ﴿So whoever wills remembers it, in honored scrolls, exalted, purified, in the hands of scribes, noble and obedient﴾ [ʿAbasa: 12–16].

Mālik said in his Muwaṭṭaʾ: "The best that I have heard in the explanation of His saying ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa: 79] is that it is like this verse in Surat ʿAbasa."

Among them: the verse is Meccan, from a Meccan surah, which includes establishing tawḥīd, prophethood, and the resurrection, affirming the Creator, and refuting the disbelievers. This meaning is more fitting to the purpose than a practical branch, which is the ruling on touching the muṣḥaf by one in a state of minor impurity.

Among them: had it been meant as the book in the hands of people, there would be little benefit in swearing this great oath on it, for it is known that every speech is capable of being in a book, true or false. Unlike when the oath falls on its being in a well-guarded Book, hidden from eyes with Allah, which no devil reaches, and which none touches except pure, purified spirits.

This meaning is more fitting, more exalted, more deserving of the verse, and undoubtedly more apt.

I heard Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah sanctify his spirit, say: "However, the verse indicates, by its allusion, that the muṣḥaf is not touched except by one who is pure. For if those scrolls are not touched except by the purifiers, because of their honor with Allah, then these scrolls are all the more worthy that none touch them except one who is pure."

And I heard him say regarding the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "Angels do not enter a house in which there is a dog or a picture." If the angels, who are created beings, are prevented from entering the house by a dog and a picture, then how shall the knowledge of Allah, exalted and mighty is He, His love, the sweetness of His remembrance, and intimacy with His nearness enter a heart filled with the dogs of desires and their pictures? This is from the correct indication of the wording.

(Section)

The matter sworn to here is His saying ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾.

An interjection came between the oath and its response with His saying ﴿And indeed it is a great oath, if you only knew﴾. Within this interjection another interjection came between the attribute and the thing described, in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿if you only knew﴾. This interjection within an interjection is the most delicate and the most excellent in its placement. An interjection is at its best when it carries emphasis, an alert, or a safeguard, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds—We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity; those are the companions of Paradise, therein they will abide forever﴾.

So He interjected between the subject and the predicate with ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾, because it contains a safeguard that repels the assumption of one who might think that the promise is owed only to one who has brought all the righteous deeds; so this was removed by ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾.

This is better than the view of those who said that it is a predicate about "those who believe," and then a second predicate was given about them, so that they would be two predicates about one subject. For the absence of burdening beyond capacity is not specific to those who believe; it is a ruling that encompasses all creation. Moreover, that assumption leaves the predicate without a connecting pronoun, requires positing a deleted attribute (i.e., "a soul from among them"), and nullifies this great benefit.

(Section)

Then He said ﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾, describing it with what requires its goodness, the abundance of its good and its benefits, and its greatness. Al-karīm (noble) is that which is radiant, abundant in good, and great in benefit, and it is, of every thing, the best and most excellent of it. Allah, glorified is He, described Himself as noble (karīm), described His speech with it, described His Throne with it, and described with it that which abounds in good and is pleasant to behold, such as plants and other things. For this reason the early scholars (al-salaf) explained karīm as "good." Al-Kalbī said: "Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an" means "good, noble before Allah." Muqātil said: "Allah ennobled it and made it honored, because it is His speech." Al-Azharī said: "Al-karīm is a comprehensive term for what is praised, and Allah is karīm, beautiful in His acts. And indeed it is a noble Qur'an, praised for the guidance, clarity, knowledge, and wisdom in it."

In sum, the karīm is one who by nature gives much good with ease and facility, and its opposite is the lāʾim (base, ignoble), who does not bring forth even a little of his good except with difficulty and hardship. Likewise, the karīm among people and the lāʾim.

(Section)

Then He, exalted is He, said ﴿in a Book well-guarded﴾.

The exegetes differed regarding this. It was said that it is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ). The correct view is that it is the Book that is in the hands of the angels, which is the one mentioned in His saying ﴿in honored scrolls, exalted, purified, in the hands of scribes, noble and obedient﴾.

What shows that it is the Book in the hands of the angels is His saying ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾. This indicates that it is in their hands, and they touch it. This is the correct meaning of the verse. Among the exegetes is one who said that what is meant is that the muṣḥaf (the codex) is touched only by one who is in a state of purity.

The first view is more likely, for several reasons:

First: the verse was brought to declare the Qur'an free from being brought down by the devils, and that its place—none touches it except the purified. It is impossible for the most wicked and impure of Allah's creatures to reach it or touch it, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The devils did not bring it down, nor is it befitting for them, nor are they able to.﴾ He negated the act, its being fitting for them, and their ability to do it. They did not do it, it is not fitting for them, and they are not able to. For an act may be negated from one who would be capable of it, and may be fitting for one who is not able to do it. So He negated these three matters from them. Likewise His saying in Surat ʿAbasa: ﴿in honored scrolls, exalted, purified, in the hands of scribes, noble and obedient﴾. Among them: this is a report. Had it been a prohibition, it would have been "lā yamassuhu" with a jussive. The basic principle of a report is that it is a report in form and in meaning.

Among them: this is a refutation of one who said that the devil brought this Qur'an. So He, exalted is He, reported that it is in a Book well-guarded, which the devils do not reach; there is no way for them to it, as He, exalted is He, said in the verse of al-Shuʿarāʾ: ﴿And the devils did not bring it down, nor is it befitting for them, nor are they able [to]﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 210–211]. Only the purified spirits reach it, and they are the angels.

Among them: this is parallel to the verse in Surat ʿAbasa: ﴿So whoever wills remembers it, in honored scrolls, exalted, purified, in the hands of scribes, noble and obedient﴾ [ʿAbasa: 12–16].

Among them: the verse is Meccan, from a Meccan surah, which includes establishing tawḥīd, prophethood, and the resurrection, affirming the Creator, and refuting the disbelievers. This meaning is more fitting to the purpose than a practical branch, which is the ruling on touching the muṣḥaf by one in a state of minor impurity.

Among them: had it been meant as the book in the hands of people, there would be little benefit in swearing this great oath on it, for it is known that every speech is capable of being in a book, true or false. This meaning is more fitting, more exalted, more deserving of the verse, and undoubtedly more apt.

And I heard him say regarding the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "Angels do not enter a house in which there is a dog or a picture." This is from the correct indication of the wording.

(Fasl)

Then He emphasized this, confirmed it and made it firm by His saying: ﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾

Just as it is necessarily tied to its being a noble Qur'an in a protected Book, it also necessitates it: it is an indicator of it and what it indicates.

Its being a revelation from the Lord of the worlds yields two great objectives from among the most important objectives of the religion.

The first: that He is the Speaker, that it was sent down from Him, that it originated from Him, and that He is the One who spoke it. From this the early scholars (al-salaf) said: "It originated from Him." A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿But the word has come into effect from Me﴾ and His saying: ﴿Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down from your Lord.﴾

Descent and sending down, as reason conceives it and as natural disposition recognizes it, is the arrival of a thing from a higher place to a lower one. The Lord, exalted is He, addresses His servants only in what their natural dispositions recognize and their intellects bear witness to. He mentioned the sending down attributed to His lordship over the worlds, which entails His ownership of them, His disposal over them, His judgment upon them, and His benevolence and blessings upon them. How could it befit One with such a relationship to creation, with His complete lordship, to leave them neglected, to abandon them purposeless, and to create them in vain, not commanding them, not forbidding them, not rewarding them, and not punishing them? This argument is stronger and more noble than argument by miracles and extraordinary events, although the latter's indication is closer to the minds of ordinary people, while the former is for the elite of the intelligent.

Allah has pointed to both methods in more than one place in His Book, such as His saying: ﴿We shall show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves, until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.﴾ This is argument from observed created signs. Then He said: ﴿Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is a witness over all things?﴾

This is argument from the perfection of His lordship and the perfection of His attributes to the truthfulness of His Messenger in what he brought. This method is more particular, stronger, more complete and higher. The first is more general and comprehensive. Its explanation has already passed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾. How far is the argument from the attributes of the Lord, exalted is He, and His holy perfection, to the establishment of the Prophet and his sending, from the argument for it through some of His creatures!

Consider the difference between the argument of the mistress of the women of the worlds, Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her, from the attributes of the Lord, exalted is He, and the attributes of Muhammad, and her deduction from between these two matters the soundness of his prophethood, that he is truly the Messenger of Allah, and that One whose attributes are these, the Lord and Creator of such a man, refuses to disgrace him, that He supports him, exalts him, and completes His blessing upon him.

If you reflect upon this method and this argument, you will find between it and the method of the theologians (al-mutakallimun) a difference that is not hidden. When a servant gains understanding of the Names and Attributes, he benefits greatly and most completely from it in the matter of recognizing truth and falsehood among statements, methods, doctrines and creeds. We have already made clear in our book al-Ma'alim the invalidity of tahayyul (evasion) and other divine stratagems concerning the Names and Attributes of the Lord, and that it is impossible for the Wise to forbid a thing and threaten its doer with the gravest punishments, and then permit reaching it by its own means through various stratagems. For that severe threat and the permissibility of reaching it by a remote route are incompatible, since the wisdom of the Lord, the perfection of His knowledge, and His Names and Attributes are not undone by the supposition of such a thing or its impossibility for Him. This is an argument from the greater jurisprudence concerning the Names and Attributes to the practical jurisprudence concerning the domain of command and prohibition. This is a domain forbidden to the Jahmi who negates attributes, that he should enter Paradise: its fragrance is forbidden to him, though its fragrance is indeed perceived from a distance of fifty thousand years. And Allah is the Mighty, the Bestower; none can withhold what He gives, and none can give what He withholds. And success is from Allah.

(Section)

Then He (glory be to Him) rebuked them for placing their softening (of position) in other than its proper place, for they were softening towards that which should be proclaimed openly, distinguished by, and held fast to with the molars, around which the fingers are folded and in which hearts and minds are bound. It is that for the sake of which one wages war and makes peace, from which one does not swerve right or left, and to which the heart does not turn to anything else; it is the only judge, the only means of contention, the only guide in the paths of lofty aims, and the only cure. It is the spirit of existence, the life of the world, the axis of happiness, the leader to success, the way to salvation, the path of right guidance, and the light of insight. So how can softening be sought with that which is of this nature? It was not sent down for softening; it was sent down with the truth and for the truth. Softening occurs only regarding a strong falsehood that cannot be removed, or regarding a weak truth that cannot be established, so the one who softens must leave off some of the truth and adhere to some of the falsehood. As for the truth by which every truth is established, how could one soften regarding it?

Then He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny it.﴾

Since the sustenance of each of the body and the heart is sustained only by provision, the provision of the body is food and drink, and the provision of the heart is faith, knowledge of its Lord and Originator, love for Him, longing for Him, intimacy with His nearness, and delight in His remembrance. Just as the body has no life except through food and drink, the heart has no life except through these. God (glory be to Him) blessed His servants with these two kinds of provision and made the sustaining of their bodies and hearts depend on them. Then, in distributing these two provisions, He (glory be to Him) varied among them according to what His knowledge and wisdom required: among them are those whose share of both provisions is abundant and whose means are broadened in both; among them are those whose provision is constricted in both; and among them are those whose bodily provision is broadened while their heart's provision is constricted, and vice versa. This provision is only completed and perfected through gratitude, and gratitude is the source of its increase and the cause of its preservation and continuance, while abandoning gratitude is the cause of its removal and cutting off from the servant. God Most High has decreed that He will surely increase the favors of the grateful, and will surely take away the favors of those who do not give thanks for them. So when they put disbelief and denial in the place of gratitude and faith, they made their very provision a denial. Since belief and gratitude are the cause of the increase of provision, and they are in reality the provision of the heart, these people instead made denial and disbelief their portion, so they made their provision denial. This is the meaning that those who said the sense is "and you make the gratitude for your provision that you deny" were circling around; and others said the sense is "and you make, in place of the gratitude for your provision, that you deny," deleting two annexed words together. These latter lengthened the wording and fell short in meaning. And among those who gave a partial sense of the verse is the saying "we were given rain by such-and-such a star-fall," but this cannot be indicated by the verse; otherwise its meaning is broader, more general, and higher. And God knows best.

(Benefit)

His saying: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny it﴾ means: you make your share of this provision, by which your life is sustained, to be denial of it.

Al-Hasan said: "You make your share and portion of the Qur'an to be denial. And a servant who has no share of the Book of God except denial of it is a loser."

(Fa'ida)

Here he mentions the rulings concerning souls at death, and at the beginning of the surah he mentioned their rulings on the Great Day of Return. He placed this before that, giving precedence to the ultimate end for emphasis, since it is more important and more fitting to mention. (Fasl)

Then he concluded the surah with their conditions at the Lesser Resurrection, just as he mentioned at its beginning their conditions at the Greater Resurrection, and he divided them into three categories, just as he divided them into three there. Before this division he presented proof of its soundness and validity: that they are created, managed, and owned, and that above them is a Lord, Subduer, Owner, who disposes of them according to His will and desire. He confronted them with this in a way they have no means to repel or deny. So He said: ﴿Why then, when it [the soul] reaches the throat﴾, meaning: when the soul has reached this point, where it has departed yet has not departed, so it is a barrier (barzakh) between death and life, just as when it has departed it is in a barrier between this world and the Hereafter. The angels of the Lord, exalted is He, are closer to the dying person than those present among mankind, but you do not see them. ﴿Why then do you not return it [to its place], if you are not to be recompensed, nor held accountable?﴾ O present ones, if the matter is as you claim, that you are not to be requited, nor held to account, nor brought to the Day of Reckoning.

If it is said: What connection is there between these two matters, that one is necessarily tied to the other?

It is said: This is among the best and most eloquent of proofs. For they either acknowledge that they are created, owned, servants of a Owner who is capable, disposing over them, Subduer, commander and forbidder, or they do not acknowledge this. If they acknowledge it, then it is incumbent upon them to fulfil His right over them, to thank Him, to exalt and glorify Him, and not to set up rivals or partners with Him. This is what His Messenger brought them and what His Book was revealed with. If they deny this and say they are not servants, nor owned, nor created, and that the matter is in their hands, then (let them) return the souls to their resting places when they reach the throat. For one who disposes of himself and rules over his own soul cannot be prevented from this, unlike the one who is ruled over, disposed of, and not the one who manages it, namely the servant owned in every respect. This proof is inescapable and irrefutable. Whoever gives it its due in affirmation and explanation benefits from it to the utmost, submits to servanthood because of it, yields, and cannot do other than submit to Lordship and Divinity and acknowledge servanthood. How excellent is the solidity and eloquence of these expressions, and how they reach the furthest degrees of rhetoric, eloquence, and complete brevity, and call to their meaning from the nearest place, and include rebuke, confrontation, and obligation, and the proofs of Lordship, Oneness, Resurrection, and the decisive resolution of the dispute regarding knowledge of the soul, that it ascends and descends and moves from place to place. How excellent is the repetition of "why then" (lawlā) a second time before mentioning the action it requires, and making the two particles require it with a single requirement, and mentioning the two conditions separated by a single word that links the first and second "why then" and the first and second conditions. This is a construction that astonishes both reason and hearing in its meaning and its wording.

Thus the two verses comprise confrontation, rebuke, proof, and establishment of the foundations of faith: the existence of the Creator, glorified is He, the perfection of His power, the execution of His will, His Lordship, and His disposal over the souls of His servants, for they have no power to dispose of them in any way; their souls are in His hand, He takes them when He wills and returns them to them when He wills, and He empties their bodies of them at times and brings them together with them at other times. They also establish the Return, the truthfulness of His Messenger in what he reported from Him, the existence of His angels, and the affirmation of the servanthood of creation. He brought this in the form of two urgings, two rebukes, two confrontations, two answers, two conditions, and two consequents, arranged in the most excellent order and interlocked in the most excellent way, each connected to the other.

This is speech that no human being can match in its arrangement or its meaning.

Al-Farra' said: "Both ﴿why then, when it reaches the throat﴾ and ﴿why then, if you are not to be recompensed﴾ are answered by a single answer, which is ﴿you return it, if you are truthful﴾."

He said: "Similar to this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then if there comes to you guidance from Me, whoever follows My guidance, there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾."

Both have a single answer, though they are two conditions. Al-Jurjani said: "His saying ﴿you return it﴾ is the answer to His saying ﴿why then﴾, both the earlier and the later, according to the interpretation: why then, when the soul reaches the throat, do you not return it to its place, if you are not to be held accountable nor recompensed as you claim?" The Exalted says: if the matter is as you claim, that there is no resurrection, no reckoning, no recompense, and no god or lord who manages that, then why do you not return the soul of one who is dear to you when it reaches the throat? Since you have no means of doing so in any way, does this not show you that the matter belongs to a sovereign, Capable, Subduer, who disposes over you, namely Allah, there is no god but He?

Abu Ishaq said: its meaning is: "Why then do you not return the soul, if you are not owned and managed? Why then, if the matter is as you claim—as your speaker says: ﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed﴾ and ﴿If they had been with us, they would not have died or been killed﴾." That is: if you are able to delay a term, why then do you not return the soul when it reaches the throat, and why do you not turn away death from yourselves?

I say: It seems this alludes to His saying: ﴿Say: Be stones or iron, or a creation of what is greater in your breasts﴾.

That is: if you claim that you will not be resurrected after death as a new creation, then become a creation that does not perish nor decay, whether of stone, or iron, or something greater than that. The connection is what has been mentioned before: either you acknowledge that you have a Lord who disposes over you and owns you, whose will and power are executed over you, who causes you to die when He wills and gives you life when He wills; then how do you deny His power to restore you as a new creation after He has caused you to die? Or you deny that you have a Lord who is Capable, Subduer, Owner, whose will and power are executed over you; then become a creation that does not accept perishing and death. Since you cannot be such, what do you deny of the power of the One who made you a creation that dies and lives, that He should give you life after He has caused you to die? This is a proof that defeats them in not being a creation that does not die. What is in the event is a proof that defeats them in returning the soul to its place when it has come near death. After this proof there remains nothing but submission and yielding, or disbelief and obstinacy.

This proof is inescapable and irrefutable. Whoever gives it its due in affirmation and explanation benefits from it to the utmost, submits to servanthood because of it, yields, and cannot do other than submit to Lordship and Divinity and acknowledge servanthood. How excellent is the solidity and eloquence of these expressions, and how they reach the furthest degrees of rhetoric, eloquence, and complete brevity, and call to their meaning from the nearest place, and include rebuke, confrontation, and obligation, and the proofs of Lordship, Oneness, Resurrection, and the decisive resolution of the dispute regarding knowledge of the soul, that it ascends and descends and moves from place to place. How excellent is the repetition of "why then" (lawlā) a second time before mentioning the action it requires, and making the two particles require it with a single requirement, and mentioning the two conditions separated by a single word that links the first and second "why then" and the first and second conditions. This is a construction that astonishes both reason and hearing in its meaning and its wording.

Thus the two verses comprise confrontation, rebuke, proof, and establishment of the foundations of faith: the existence of the Creator, glorified is He, the perfection of His power, the execution of His will, His Lordship, and His disposal over the souls of His servants, for they have no power to dispose of them in any way; their souls are in His hand, He takes them when He wills and returns them to them when He wills, and He empties their bodies of them at times and brings them together with them at other times. They also establish the Return, the truthfulness of His Messenger in what he reported from Him, the existence of His angels, and the affirmation of the servanthood of creation. He brought this in the form of two urgings, two rebukes, two confrontations, two answers, two conditions, and two consequents, arranged in the most excellent order and interlocked in the most excellent way, each connected to the other.

This is speech that no human being can match in its arrangement or its meaning.

Al-Farra' said: "Both ﴿why then, when it reaches the throat﴾ and ﴿why then, if you are not to be recompensed﴾ are answered by a single answer, which is ﴿you return it, if you are truthful﴾."

He said: "Similar to this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿Then if there comes to you guidance from Me, whoever follows My guidance, there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾."

Both have a single answer, though they are two conditions. Al-Jurjani said: "His saying ﴿you return it﴾ is the answer to His saying ﴿why then﴾, both the earlier and the later, according to the interpretation: why then, when the soul reaches the throat, do you not return it to its place, if you are not to be held accountable nor recompensed as you claim?" The Exalted says: if the matter is as you claim, that there is no resurrection, no reckoning, no recompense, and no god or lord who manages that, then why do you not return the soul of one who is dear to you when it reaches the throat? Since you have no means of doing so in any way, does this not show you that the matter belongs to a sovereign, Capable, Subduer, who disposes over you, namely Allah, there is no god but He?

Abu Ishaq said: its meaning is: "Why then do you not return the soul, if you are not owned and managed? Why then, if the matter is as you claim—as your speaker says: ﴿If they had obeyed us, they would not have been killed﴾ and ﴿If they had been with us, they would not have died or been killed﴾." That is: if you are able to delay a term, why then do you not return the soul when it reaches the throat, and why do you not turn away death from yourselves?

I say: It seems this alludes to His saying: ﴿Say: Be stones or iron, or a creation of what is greater in your breasts﴾.

That is: if you claim that you will not be resurrected after death as a new creation, then become a creation that does not perish nor decay, whether of stone, or iron, or something greater than that. The connection is what has been mentioned before: either you acknowledge that you have a Lord who disposes over you and owns you, whose will and power are executed over you, who causes you to die when He wills and gives you life when He wills; then how do you deny His power to restore you as a new creation after He has caused you to die? Or you deny that you have a Lord who is Capable, Subduer, Owner, whose will and power are executed over you; then become a creation that does not accept perishing and death. Since you cannot be such, what do you deny of the power of the One who made you a creation that dies and lives, that He should give you life after He has caused you to die? This is a proof that defeats them in not being a creation that does not die. What is in the event is a proof that defeats them in returning the soul to its place when it has come near death. After this proof there remains nothing but submission and yielding, or disbelief and obstinacy.

That is, why do you not return the soul to its place, if you are not subject to a Lord, subdued, or recompensed? This verse requires explanation (tafsir). It was brought as an argument against them for their denial of the resurrection (al-ba'th) and the reckoning (al-hisab). A proof must necessarily imply what it proves, such that the mind passes from it to what is proven, because of the necessary connection between them. Thus the thing that necessitates is a proof of what it necessitates, but the converse is not required.

The line of argument is this: when they deny the resurrection and the recompense, they have disbelieved in their Lord and denied His power, His lordship, and His wisdom. They must then either acknowledge that they have a Lord who is dominant and who disposes of them as He wills, causing them to die when He wishes and bringing them to life when He wishes, commanding them and forbidding them, rewarding the good among them and punishing the wrongdoers. Or they must deny that there is a Lord of this description. If they acknowledge Him, they must believe in the resurrection, the rising, and the religion of command and recompense. If they deny Him, they have disbelieved in Him, and they claim that they are not subject to a Lord, not under any rule, and that there is no Lord who disposes of them as He wills. Then why are they not able to repel death from themselves when it comes to them, and to return the soul to its resting place when it reaches the throat? This is addressed to those present, who are at the bedside of the dying person and see his death with their own eyes. That is, why do you not return the soul to its place, if you have power and authority, and you are not subject to a dominant, capable Lord whose judgments take effect over you and whose commands are carried out? This is the utmost challenge to them, for it shows their inability to return a single soul to its place, even if both humans and jinn were to gather together for that purpose. **(Section)**

The ninth stage of the stages of life is the life of the spirits after their separation from the bodies and their release from this prison and its constriction. Behind it is spaciousness, rest, rayhan, and ease. The relation of this abode to that life is like the relation of the mother's womb to this abode, or closer than that.

One of the knowers (al-arifin) said: "Let your hastening to leave this world be like your hastening to leave a narrow prison to go to your beloved ones and gather with them in the radiant gardens."

Allah the Exalted said about this life: ﴿And as for if he is of those brought near, then rest and rayhan and a Garden of Delight﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 88].

What suffices for the goodness of this life is companionship with the Highest Companion (al-Rafiq al-A'la), and separation from the harmful, troublesome companion whose sight and presence spoil life, let alone associating and living with him. I said, when they praised life and went to excess:
"In death are a thousand virtues that are unknown,
Among them the assurance of meeting Him through meeting Him, and the parting from every companion who does not deal fairly."

And if death had no good in it except that it is the door of entry into this life and a bridge crossed to it, it would suffice as a gift for the believer.

May Allah reward death on our behalf with good, for it is kinder to us than every kindness and gentler.
It hastens the release of souls from harm, and brings them near to the abode that is more noble.

So striving in this short life, in this brief span, and the effort, toil, bearing of burdens, weariness, and hardship, is only for this life. Knowledge and deeds are means toward it. This (the afterlife) is wakefulness, while what precedes it of life is sleep. This is the eye, while what precedes it is a trace. This is a life that combines the absence of what is disliked with the attainment of what is loved, in the station of intimacy and the presence of holiness, where no sought thing is unattainable and no beloved is lost. There is tranquillity and rest, joy and happiness. There the servant has no expression for the reality of its essence, because it is in a land we have no acquaintance with, and there is no familiarity between us and its inhabitants. The soul, accustomed for a long time to this narrow and wretched prison, dislikes moving from it to that land, and feels estranged when it perceives its separation from this prison.

Knowledge of this life reached us only through divine information, by the hand of the most perfect, most knowing, and most sincere of creation, (ﷺ). Its evidences stood in the hearts of the people of faith until it became for them as direct sight. So their souls fled from this passing shade, this vanishing phantom, and this perishing life mixed with disturbance and kinds of distress, out of aversion to this life and longing for that dominion, desire for this joy, rapture upon this measure, and yearning for this breeze that comes from the place of lasting bliss.

By Allah's life, whoever travels to a land of justice, fertility, security, and joy, endures every hardship, scarcity, and drought along its path. He parts from those who stay behind when he most needs them, answers the caller when he calls "hasten to success," gives his soul in reaching it with the giving of a lover, willingly and generously, and continues the journey by morning and evening. He praises the night journey upon arrival, for the traveller praises the night march only at dawn.

I said:
"At dawn the people praise the night journey,
And at death the people praise the meeting."

By Allah, this is not hard or severe, given this short life, which compared to that abode is like an hour of a day: ﴿As if they, on the day they see what they were promised, had not remained but an hour of a day﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]. ﴿And the day He gathers them, as if they had not remained but an hour of the day, recognizing one another﴾ [Yunus: 45]. ﴿As if they, on the day they see it, had not remained but an evening or its morning﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 46]. ﴿And the day the Hour is established, the criminals will swear they remained not but an hour﴾ [al-Rum: 55]. ﴿He said: "How long did you remain on earth, counted in years?" They said: "We remained a day or part of a day; so ask those who count." He said: "You remained but a little, if only you had known"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 112-114].

If one of us were dragged on his face, protecting himself from thorns and stones, to this life, that would not be much, nor a loss compared with what he is spared.

Alas, for an insight that has witnessed these two lives as they truly are, and for a resolve that prefers the lower over the higher! This is only by the success of the One in whose hands are the reins of all affairs, from whom every thing begins and to whom it returns. He kept back the souls over whom wretchedness prevailed from journeying to this abode, and He drew the hearts for whom the good was previously decreed. He made them stand on the path and made the risks easy for them to ride. So those first wasted the stages of their lives with those who stayed behind, while these traversed the stages of their lives with the travellers. The dust settled, the dust storm rose, and the travellers and those who stayed behind were hidden from one another.

It will soon be cleared away: the doers will prevail, and the falsifiers will lose.

Among the goodness and delight of this life: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No soul dies that has with Allah a good reward which would please it to return to the world and have the world and all that is in it, except the martyr. He wishes to return to the world, because of what he sees of Allah's honour for him," meaning that he may be killed in it a second time.

One of the knowers heard a reciter reciting:
"Life is only in the animal enjoyment of pleasure, as the philosopher says.
The rule of the cup of death is that it makes equal in its sip the dullard and the sharp-minded,
And the ignorant becomes beneath the soil of the earth as the clever one has become beneath it.
So ask the earth about the two of them, if the clear question removes doubt and suspicion."

He said: "May Allah fight him! How intense is his opposition to religion and reason! This is the very enemy of the natural disposition (fitrah), the law (shari'ah), reason, faith, and wisdom. O poor one! Because death makes the righteous and the wicked equal, the knowing and the ignorant equal, and all of them beneath the layers of the soil, must they therefore be equal in their final outcome? Do not people who travel from one land to another, on the road, become equal? Yet when they reach their destination, each one descends into the place prepared for him, and is received differently from his companion on the road. Does not each people have a home, so that each one is seated where he deserves? Is one thing repaid with something and the other with its opposite? Has not one who came to the king with what pleases him been honoured by him, while one who came with what angers him has been punished for it? Has not a caravan arrived at the city, so that some of them dwell in its palaces, gardens, and noble places, while others remain on the roadsides among the dogs? Have not two who came from one mother's womb, one of them attained kingship while the other fell into captivity and hardship?"

As for your saying, "Ask the earth about the two of them": indeed we have asked it, and it informed us that it has gathered their bodies, their corpses, and their joints, not their disbelief and faith, nor their lineages and nobilities, nor their forbearance and folly, nor their obedience and disobedience, nor their certainty and doubt, nor their monotheism and polytheism, nor their injustice and justice, nor their knowledge and ignorance. It informed us about these decayed corpses, these dissolving bodies, and these torn joints, and said: "This is the report of what I possess."

As for the report of those spirits and what they have come to, ask about it the books of the Lord of the worlds, His truthful messengers, and their successors who inherited from them. Ask the Qur'an, for with it is the certain report. Ask the one who brought it, for he is the most knowing of the knowers of that. Ask knowledge and faith, for they are the two accepted witnesses. Ask the intellects and the natural dispositions, for with them is the reality of the report. ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think that We will make them like those who believe and do righteous deeds, equal in their living and their dying? Evil is what they judge﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 21].

Exalted is Allah, the Most Wise of judges, above this supposition and reckoning, which is fitting only for the most ignorant of the ignorant.

Then he said: "The one who looks into this subject is of two kinds: a man who looks at things, and a man who looks into things. The first is bewildered by them, for their forms, shapes, and outlines empty his mind and sense, and scatter his thought and heart. His looking at them is with the eye of sensation, and it does not benefit him with the fruit of reflection nor the essence of testing, because when he lacks reflection at first, he lacks choice second.

As for the one who looks into things, his looking leads him to pass from their forms to their realities and what is intended by them, and to what the existence of them required of profound wisdom and complete knowledge. This looking benefits him by distinguishing their ranks, knowing what benefits from what harms, the sound from the sick, the lasting from the perishing, the husk from the kernel. He distinguishes between the means and the end, and between the means of a thing and the means of its opposite. Then he knows that this world is its husk and the Hereafter is its kernel, that this world is the place of sowing and the Hereafter is the time of harvest, that this world is a crossing and a passage, and the Hereafter is the abode of settlement.

When he knows that this world is a path and a passage, he is worthy of preparing provision for his settlement. He then knows that he was not created in this abode to settle and remain forever, but to pass on to another place, which is the dwelling and the resting-place. He knows that man was called to this by every law, on the tongue of every prophet, by every sign and proof. A sign was set up for him regarding it, every example was struck for its sake, and he was alerted to it by his first origin and beginnings, and all his other states, and the states of his food and drink, his earth and sky, such that doubt was removed from him, the clear path was shown to him, the proof was established against him, and he was given the fullest excuse and granted the fullest respite. So it became clear to the one of sound intellect and upright disposition that departing from this place is necessary, that moving from it is a truth beyond doubt, and that there is for him another place for which he was created and prepared. His destination is toward it, and his arrival there is without doubt. And that his present abode is a station of passage, not a station of settlement."

In sum: whoever contemplates the existing things, and is not content with merely looking at them alone, will find them indicating that behind this life there is another life more perfect than it, and that this life, in relation to that one, is like sleep in relation to wakefulness, and like a shadow in relation to the person. He will hear them all calling out with what their Lord, their Creator and their Originator called out: ﴿O mankind, indeed the promise of Allah is true, so let not the worldly life deceive you, and let not the Deceiver deceive you concerning Allah﴾ [Fatir: 5]. They call out in the tongue of their state what their Lord called out in explicit speech. ﴿And present to them the example of the worldly life: it is like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it, and then it becomes dry stalks scattered by the winds. And Allah is ever Able to do all things﴾ [al-Kahf: 45]. And the Exalted said: ﴿The example of the worldly life is only like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it, from what people and livestock eat, until when the earth takes its adornment and is beautified, and its people think they have power over it, Our command comes to it by night or by day, and We make it into cut-down stubble as if it had not flourished yesterday. Thus do We detail the signs for a people who give thought﴾ [Yunus: 24]. And the Exalted said: ﴿Know that the worldly life is only play and amusement, adornment, boasting among you, and competition in wealth and children. It is like a rain whose plants please the disbelievers; then it dries up, and you see it turning yellow; then it becomes debris. And in the Hereafter there is severe punishment, and forgiveness from Allah and approval. And the worldly life is not but the enjoyment of delusion﴾ [al-Hadid: 20]. Then He urged them to race toward the Hereafter, the enduring abode that has no end. He said: ﴿Race to forgiveness from your Lord and a garden whose width is like the width of the heaven and the earth, prepared for those who have believed in Allah and His messengers. That is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾ [al-Hadid: 21].
